en: The preface was written by the Elder Lingyuan, Chan Master Weiqing—
otherwise known as the Ancient Pagoda Master. His pure conduct was stainless, his solitary style was beyond peer, and his reputation was held in high esteem.

In those days, [Yunmen] was truly not one who attained [enlightenment] in vain. His subtle pivot for engaging with beings pointed deeply toward awakening; his direct speech established the fundamental principle, and many in the world have investigated it.

Yet, as he judged the two articles for himself and set forth the Three Essentials and Three Mysteries—categorizing causes and conditions and distinguishing between the ordained and the laity—those of suspicious temperament have occasionally offered criticism, claiming that he had never even met Yunmen and yet publicly styled himself the legitimate successor.

This is like determining the emptiness of a vessel by following its shape, or seeking a lost sword by marking the spot on a boat; it is as if one has personally encountered the Great Medicine, yet instead aggravates a chronic ailment.

If you would reflect deeply upon this, your spiritual understanding will become clear and distinct, and you will realize that this Superior Person was certainly not acting in vain. — Chan Master Daoxuan.
Upon hearing this, I, Songtong, requested that this record be carved onto printing blocks for circulation. I further entreated him to grant me these words as a preface.
This was truly on the Mid-Autumn Day of the fourth year of the Shaosheng era.
The Village Elder of Yunmen, Miaoxi, says:
In our school of Chan, there is no transmission or bestowal. What can be transmitted and bestowed are merely the texts of the doctrinal vehicles and the words of past masters;
they are not the ultimate subtlety of the mind. That ultimate, subtle mind is valued for its realization through non-transgression of a single thought-moment. If one is indeed [as it truly is],...
Upon realization, the words of the scriptural vehicles and the speech of the former masters—neither lacking nor redundant—are all the wondrous functioning of this very mind.
It is like splitting sandalwood: every fragment is no different from the whole. Therefore it is said: "A separate transmission outside the teachings;

not establishing written words; pointing directly at the human mind; seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha. This is a discourse that remains unchanging for ten thousand generations. Lately, however, the monastic communities have been full of deception and falsehood.

Among those who follow the stream of Dharma preaching, there are those who do not believe in wondrous awakening, but instead devote themselves exclusively to the texts of the doctrinal vehicles (*śāsana-yāna*).
They seek out phrases and extract sentences from the words of past masters, using them to seduce scholars; these they transmit as family treasures.

Some take the story of the single shoe returning to the West as the "great matter" of his final moments; others take the five ranks (*pañca-sthāna*), the merits, and the interplay of the biased and the correct (*yǎng-zhèng huí-hù*) as their ancestral legacy.
Each establishes its own school and each upholds its own lineage, calling this their "fundamental tenet" (*zongzhi*).
To observe such claims, how are they different from a swarm of lice living within a garment? They flee into deep seams and hide in tattered stuffing, considering it a fortunate dwelling.
Yet when a conflagration sweeps through a scorched land, burning down towns and cities, the lice within the garment cannot escape. This is precisely what is meant by that. Linji said: "There is..."

There is a certain class of people who fail to recognize good from evil. Within the teachings of the scriptures, they grasp at the general meaning and engage in speculative deliberation to construct phrases and doctrines.

It is like taking a lump of excrement in one's hand, tasting it with the mouth, and then spitting it out to give to others. Having reflected upon these words three times, I have never failed to sigh with deep lamentation.
Alas! How might this old master be brought back to life once more, to act as an acupuncturist for the chronic ailments of those who come after him?
Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Chan Master *Fejiqu*.
Compiled by his disciple from Yuzhang, Wen Zhi.

On the third day of the tenth month in the fourth year of the Jingshou era of the Great Song dynasty, the year of Dingchou, Lord Fan, the Prefectural Administrator and Imperial Consultant, personally led the fourfold assembly to Mount Zhi to welcome the Master back to the monastery. When the Master ascended the hall and took his seat, he remained silent.
Elder An-guo then addressed the assembly, saying: "One should contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Yet the assembly still did not [understand].
[The Master] steps down and says: "Master Anguo, you were already quite disheveled just now;
this old monk cannot add further mud upon the earth. Monks, do not stand for long. He then descends from his seat.

That evening, during the evening session (*sāṃdhyika*), a monk asked: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying on conditions. As a student who has come here, I request the Master to grant me an instruction.
The Master said: "A diamond straw sandal. The monk stepped forward and said: "If that is so, then I shall retreat three steps. The Master said: "Truly, ten thousand miles away. Another monk asked:
"When humans and devas gather together and the fourfold assembly has arrived, what is the meaning of this for the Master?"

"A phrase for the sake of others. The Master said, "Clear water surges over the ripples. The student said, "A dot. The Master said, "Too much. The student clapped his hands. The Master said, "Withdraw.
The student asked, "One shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function proceed simultaneously. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Dry firewood and damp bamboo splinters. The student then gave a shout. The Master said, "Red flames blazing to the heavens."
It is further said: "When patch-robed monks meet one another, they do not involve themselves in verbal explanations. Yet, how can it be helped that worldly people are present at the gathering?
Thus, one must open a single thread of the Way. Nevertheless, even so, how does one discern and clarify this? Even if one were to perceive it with absolute clarity and precision,"
This may be attained on the level of a layperson, but on the level of a patch-robed monk (*bhikṣu*), it is worlds apart.
Great assembly, what is the matter on the level of a patch-robed monk? Try to say it! Do not say, "The coins are full-value";
do not say, "The soil is rich, but the eggplants are lazy. If you hold such a view, how are you any different from a layperson? If it is not so, then what is it?

Regarding the matter within the scope of a patch-robed monk: for those who have long studied under former masters, it requires no further words. For beginners among the later students, you must simply be thorough and careful.
There is no need to stand here for long. Take care.
The donor invited the Master for an evening discourse. A monk asked, "It is said that 'the lush green bamboo is all True Suchness (Tathatā), and the dense yellow flowers are nothing but Prajñā.
What is Prajñā? The Master said, "In the Yellow Springs, there is no old or young. The monk pressed further, "When spring comes, the grass grows green of its own accord.
The Master said, "One's reputation shall be imperishable. The monk said, "If that is so, then as for the blue-eyed barbarian monk..."
[The Master] frowned. The Master said, "Step back three paces. The student said, "It is painful. The Master said, "Hūṃ, hūṃ!
[The student] asked, "The assembly of humans and devas has gathered; we await your thunderous voice. This student has come forward; we pray that the Master will deign to speak. The Master said:
"Time flies like an arrow. The student said, "As soon as a single word is uttered, all understand;
where the incense smoke rises, all receive its grace. The Master said, "An ancient had a saying. The student gave a shout. The Master said, "Blind! The student said, "You let this one pass.
The Master said, "Before the great assembly of devas and humans, I grant you thirty blows. The Master then said:
Since I began my travels as a wandering monk, I have never before been pressed by others this year to take up residence in a monastery, open the hall, and serve as an elder (*sthavira*).
This is the one thing a patch-robed monk (*bhikṣu*) finds most disadvantageous.
From this day forward, being called an "elder" or a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) is much like having someone spit directly in one's face. Furthermore, being addressed by laypeople...
I request that you gentlemen attend the evening session. It is unavoidable that some will speak of the Buddha or the Dharma for others, while others will slander the Buddha and revile the Dharma;
this may be called "carving a wound from one's own flesh" and "laughing until the mouths of the patch-robed monks are split. All you laypeople must likewise rouse your spirits.
Do not receive [this teaching] with the superficial glosses of finger-pointing annotations. It is late; each of you should please return home.
Take care. [The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks: "One person thrusts out his head; another lets out a shout. How far apart are these two? The Master says:
"At the third watch in the middle of the night. The monk replies: "The dragon returns to the blue sea; the phoenix flies back to the vermilion mountain. The Master says: "..."
Incense is burned beneath the Northern Dipper. A question was asked: "When Linji held up his whisk and the student raised his fist, were they the same or different?

The Master said, "False words confusing the assembly. The student stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then you act according to the command. The Master said: [The text continues: "Under the Northern Dipper, incense is burned. Question: "When Linji held up his whisk and the student raised his fist, were they the same or different? Master: "False speech confuses the assembly. Student: "In that case, you act according to the command. Master: [Silence] (or as indicated by the context of the dialogue).

"End of the world, edge of the sea. The student then gave a shout. The Master said, "Hūṃ, hūṃ. The student asked, "The melody is already complete; do you permit this student to provide the counter-melody?
The Master said, "The government does not allow even a needle to pass. The student stepped forward and said, "Truly, this is the talent of Boya.
The Master said, "Look for yourself. The student clapped his hands three times. The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 18.*
"Thirty blows! The Master said: "In the presence of a patch-robed monk, it is difficult to open one's mouth.
Even if one were to utter a single word, it might cause the heavens to rain four flowers, the earth to shake in six ways, Mount Sumeru to stand upside down, and the ocean waters to boil;
yet this would still be the karmic activity of a wild fox spirit. Nevertheless, even so, you must see through it before you can attain it. If you do not understand this, then..."
One observes the thousandfold differences among things and beings: self and other, subject and object, love and hate, anger and joy, and the shifting flux of birth and death.
Therefore, the ancients said: "Exert yourself now; you must bring this to an end in this life, lest you suffer its lingering calamities for eternal eons."
On the ninth day of the first month, the hall was opened for the formal assembly. Master Fan himself composed the invitation letter, which stated:

"I humbly submit that taking 'no-mind' as the fundamental principle means there is not even a hair's breadth upon which anything can be established. To have words is itself an affliction; it is merely the forced naming of the myriad dharmas.
Now, if there is an affliction, how can it be resolved without a physician? If there is a fundamental principle, how can it be realized without a teacher?"
The Venerable Master of Ancient Virtue is pure in conduct and free from defilement; his solitary style is beyond peer. When the Dharma drum sounds once, all who hear it stand in awe;
when the divine pearl shines in the four directions, nothing remains hidden or unmanifest. As the multitude turns toward him with aspiration, he may now reveal the True Vehicle for all to behold.
"This is identical to the Tathāgata. Respectfully submitted.
This is the memorial of Fan Zhongyan, Imperial Academician of the Longtu Pavilion and Prefectural Governor of Raoyang.

Having finished reading the memorial, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "This mountain monk has received the firm command of the Prefectural Lord; today may be called the day he has cast off his jewels."
As for his robes: he wore tattered and soiled garments that closely resembled the weaponry of the state, using them only as a last resort.
He then ascended the seat and offered incense, saying: "Tell me, for whom is this single offering of incense intended? When I first set out on my travels as a monk..."
First, I visited the Venerable Daigu Kigen. This monk sat amidst the wild weeds.
Later, I visited the Venerable Ryōga of Fukugen-ji on Mount Nangaku. This monk was likewise a truly liberated patch-robed monk.
This incense is not for the sake of Venerable Daigu, nor is it for the sake of Venerable Fukugen; O Great Assembly!
Take note. There is only the Great Master Kuangzhen of Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyou Prefecture who is slightly superior to this son.
This single portion of incense, for now, I shall burn for the Great Master Kuangzhen of Yunmen Mountain. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged. The Rector struck the gavel and said:
"O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma banquet, you should contemplate the primary truth. The Master said: "The assembly, the Rector has spoken thus."

I ask you, Great Assembly: do you still find this sweet? Why? If we judge it from the perspective of the Great Assembly itself, even if all the Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would still be merely deceiving themselves;
the Patriarchs’ coming from the West was but a delusion for the mediocre and small-minded, while as for the rest of you, there is no need to even mention them.
If one were to discuss the profound or explain the essential, it would be much like spitting blood at others; if questions and answers are exchanged, it is just like [the following]:
Māra’s Disturbance. Zen Master, before this great assembly, how do you open your mouth? Although it is thus, affairs are not of a single direction; principle unfolds in a hundred ways.
For the sake of those with inferior capacities, I have spoken circuitously. If you have doubts, please ask. A monk asked: "The monkey carries its young back to the green peaks;
the bird carries fallen flowers before the azure cliffs. This is the realm of Jia Shan; which one is Jianfu?"
The Master said, "Do not. The student asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "Do not ask.
[The student said,] "I know that you have long harbored a treasure in your bag; today, at this assembly, I shall borrow it briefly to look upon it.
The Master said, "Do not. The student asked, "Is there no expedient means? The Master said, "Do not ask. When a Great Good Knowledge appears in the world, with what will he act?"
The Master said, "Do not. Jin said, "In that case, there is questioning and answering. The Master said, "Do not.
A monk was about to pose a question when the Master said, "Stop your questioning. Even if you could ask and answer, it would still be far removed from the Way.
Great assembly, even if several of you monks were to engage in such questioning, none of you would have reached the point of emergence."

"The family's eyes and ears remain here. If there were such 'eyes and ears' among those who have left the household life, they would hear that a *kalyāṇamitra* has appeared in the world ten thousand *li* away, yet they would wash their ears, knit their brows, and brush off their sleeves to flee far away. How could they ever be willing to come here, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and ask, 'How is it?
What is it? Benevolent ones, do you know? Within each and every one of you in the great assembly, what exactly is this?"
The "Mo" gate—what kind of principle is this? It is such that all Buddhas cannot look up to it, and the patriarchs of the world have no choice but to keep their mouths shut.
If one can see clearly in this way, then Buddhas and patriarchs are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky;
hearing the most profound Dharma gates is like the sound of the wind or an echo in a valley. One’s own nature becomes liberated and stands out alone, just like...
When all sentient beings within the quiescent Dharma-realm attain perfect enlightenment together, is this not the mark of a true great man? Is this not the mark of a genuine renunciant?

Setting aside these matters for a moment: though my accumulated virtues are not lofty and my turn toward the Way is not yet distant, I have sought refuge in the clouds and mountains until years and months have dimmed my countenance. I humbly acknowledge that...

To the Prefectural Waitzhi, the Director of the Bureau of Revenue, and all officials of various ranks: We have received your gracious letter and decree, ordering us to open the hall and expound the Dharma so that all may share in its blessings.

We pray for the longevity of His Majesty the Emperor, as enduring as the mountains and as bright as the sun and moon. May the civil and military officials ascend to high positions of honor and prosperity.

The venerable elders of the various monasteries, the members of the Sangha Council, and all the lay donors have from the beginning provided mutual support and assembly; I dare not delay the proclamation [of this matter] and have long suppressed my own official status.
I humbly pray that you will take care of yourselves.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Since entering this monastery, many laypeople have requested that I hold evening sermons (*wanzan*).
I can only provide such facilities according to the times and accommodate their karmic conditions. However, from the perspective of this mountain monk, it is a distinct tradition of its own. Why?

Because during my youth, while traveling to study under various masters, I visited the foremost venerable elders. Some would cite the sutras and treatises, or discourse on form and emptiness within the three realms."
Mind-only. All phenomena are but consciousness. Only thus can one attain the shared root of heaven and earth and the single substance of all phenomena.
The myriad forms may be rolled up or unfurled; the dense array of existence may be granted or withheld. All matters resound clearly, and everything manifests as it is.

Some speak of the pivotal mechanism of the "upward direction," which penetrates through the Dharma-body; therein, words do not unfold events, and speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded. Regarding this—
One who has attained clarity is a truly free and easy monk. Relying on nothing at all, he speaks exclusively of dry, unadorned Chan.
Whenever a question is posed, he does not engage in verbal exchange; instead, he may speak of the functioning of the whole body, where teaching and transformation proceed in tandem.

The host and guest, letting go and seizing; illumination and function, vertical and horizontal—within three years, all were simultaneously penetrated by this old monk and taken as the true regulations of the ancestral Way.
Later, when he himself saw through them, he realized they were all nothing more than ghostly interpretations of firefly light, which in the school of the High Ancestors is regarded as a poison.
Yet now it is widely practiced throughout the four seas; for this reason, the ancestral seats have fallen into desolation and the practitioners of the Way are silent and few.
"Virtuous ones, you must simply reflect upon this. Do not allow yourselves to be deceived. Just consider the matter according to the person concerned:

what kind of principle is this? Take care. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The mouth is the gate that invites calamity; the tongue is the axe that fells the self. If there is a monk who comes forward..."
"Drag this old monk down from his meditation seat and give him a sound beating; would that not be avenging the shame for the assembly?
I might then grant you the possession of one eye. But now, if you intend to remain here, standing with hands folded in mutual dullness, when will there ever be an end to it? Take care."

The assembly gathers for the midday meal; the Dharma-eye treasury of the Tathāgata, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch and handed down from Buddha to Buddha.

Ordinary beings and sages are equal; there is no need to seek it elsewhere. With its myriad virtues perfectly luminous, how could it require cultivation or realization? Today, this mountain monk presents it directly to your faces:
if you awaken to it, you shall immediately ascend to the stage of Buddhahood without traversing the rungs of a ladder; if you are deluded by it, you turn your back on it.

Awakening is the union with sensory objects; it is a delusion to enter the various realms of existence. There is an inherent distinction between delusion and awakening, yet this Dharma is fundamentally without increase or decrease.
Those who have long studied and attained realization share this same proof. For those of later learning and beginners, if there are doubts, you may ask.
A monk asked: "I have heard the Master say that things are presented face-to-face. What is the matter of being presented face-to-face? The Master said: "Do not..."
The student said, “Yes. The Master said, “Do not. The student said, “Yes, yes. The Master said, “Do not, do not.

Just as a monk was about to pose a question, the Master said, “Stop your questioning; it is far removed from the Way. According to your own capacities, even if you possessed unimpeded eloquence, you would still be at a loss.
A single movement of thought is already a deviation; how much more so when it takes the form of words? The assembly [was silent].

The cycle of birth and death flows on without ceasing because of the existence of the mind. If one can attain the state where not even a single thought arises, one will certainly stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddha.

Above and below the heavens, there is none more supreme; majestic and dignified, one walks alone throughout the ten directions. Responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings, there is nowhere one does not reach;
therefore, this is called "unconditioned compassion" (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and is also termed the "uninvited friend. [This state] has not yet been attained...
Thus it is. You have fallen into a deviant path.
Take heed. [The Master] ascends the hall. As soon as the drum sounds and the assembly has gathered, he leaves this mountain monk with no place to set his teeth.
Do not take offense at the ancients who said: "Ten times I intend to speak, nine times I stop. Why? Even if one were able to speak, it would be like throwing [a stone into the void].
The earth makes the sound of gold; it has no connection whatsoever with the realm of ordinary people.
Great assembly, do you wish to attain intimacy? Speak for yourselves! How will you speak? Before you have opened your mouths, there is still some margin;
the moment you open your mouths, it is all self-deception. Do not see such words spoken and immediately come forward to perform three prostrations, or—
Raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye; shaking one's sleeves and walking out; or perhaps striking with a staff or shouting—these all become irrelevant.

Aside from these, how would you speak? If you can speak here, then your leaving home and traveling on pilgrimage will not have been in vain, and you alone will be able to perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem.
If you cannot speak it, you must simply leave home. Take care.
The Master, during the early morning assembly, addressed the congregation, saying: "O Great Assembly, the frost is cold; do not trouble yourselves to stand for long. Take care.

On the day of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "To maintain the precepts and to commit transgressions are matters for beginners. As for the rules of the summer retreat, they may be known.
But if you are a guest under our gate, when we meet in the forest, we shall not raise an eyebrow."
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Great assembly, the Great Master Yunmen Kuangzhen is present right now.
Do you all see him? If you can see him, then you are fellow students of this mountain monk. See? See? This matter must be realized with absolute certainty;
one must not deceive oneself. For instance, in ancient times, when Huangbo heard Venerable Baizhang cite the Great Master Mazu—"

Regarding the circumstances of the "Lowering of the Staff" (xiàhè): through this, the other [Huangbo] gained great insight. Baizhang asked, "In the future, will you not take the Great Master as your successor?

Huangbo replied, "Although I recognize the Great Master, I have not yet seen the Great Master. If I were to take the Great Master as my successor," [he would be taking one who is not yet fully realized].
"I fear I shall lose my descendants, O Great Assembly! At that time, it had not been five years since Master Mazu passed away, yet Huangbo claimed he had never seen him.
You should know that Huangbo’s realization was not complete; at best, he possessed but a single eye. I, however, am not like this:
I have recognized Master Yunmen, and I have also seen Master Yunmen; only then can one truly receive [the Dharma]."
As for succeeding the Great Master Yunmen: it has already been over a hundred years since Yunmen entered extinction.
How can one speak now of the principle of having personally seen him? Do you understand? Only those who are penetrating and enlightened can verify this;
as for those of inferior capacity, they will surely give rise to doubt and slander. For those who have seen it, there is no need for words; for those who have not yet seen it—
"Look at this now! Do not ask me to stand for long; take care. He ascended the hall.
"Although the assembly gathers morning and evening, there are no words or phrases to lead people to understanding.
There are no words or phrases to lead people to investigate. There is no 'gate-style' (men-feng) to lead people to establish. It is simply [to be with] all of you..."
People must discern between the heterodox and the orthodox to avoid recklessly accepting [the teachings] and claiming to have attained what they have not yet attained.
This is because within the Gate of the Patriarchs' Way, men of immeasurable capacity easily understand [the truth].

For instance, in the past, we personally saw such venerable masters as Yunmen, whose great reputation was second to none—such as Deshan Mi, Dongshan Chu, Zhimen Kuan, and Baling Jian—even though they were [all deeply realized].
Regarding Yunmen: he only managed to awaken to Yunmen’s verbal teachings, yet fundamentally did not awaken to the Way or see his own nature.
How do we know this? For instance, when a monk asked Master Jian, "What is the school of Deva? Jian replied, "Silver bowls filled with snow.
Again, [the monk] asked, "What is the 'blow-off-hair' sword? Jian replied, "Coral branches supporting the moon, branch after branch. Furthermore...
Question: "Are the Buddha's teachings and the Patriarchs' teachings the same or different? Jian said: "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree;
when the duck is cold, it enters the water. Master Jian said: "I have already repaid Yunmen’s kindness by offering these three turns of words.
Henceforth, I shall no longer provide memorial services for Yunmen. "Venerable assembly, Yunmen clearly stated: 'If this matter were contained within words and phrases...'"
The Great Canon of Teachings—how could it be devoid of words and phrases? Furthermore, it is said: "Even if you can ask and can answer, you will only win a slippery tongue;
you will move further away from the Way. How does one produce the three successive turns of speech? It is then said: "I have repaid Yunmen’s kindness."

One might say this is to bury one’s ancestors and mislead future generations; it causes descendants to inherit the void and confront the precipice, passing from error to error, all claiming that mere words and phrases constitute the ultimate realization of the supreme path. O Assembly!

If you rely on the matters within such words and phrases, they are like the light of a firefly; yet within the capacity of each of you, they are like hundreds of thousands of suns and moons. O Assembly! Have you ever...?
Those who seek entry through words and phrases must quickly spit them out. Examine and scrutinize within your own being:
what principle is this? Be careful.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To cure an illness, one does not need a donkey to carry the medicine.
Then he descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, he said: "Both of you are renunciants; how then is there the eye of renunciation?
If you have not yet attained the eye of renunciation, rely for now on the definitive teachings of the Buddha, and do not rely on the non-definitive teachings. What are the non-definitive teachings?"
To speak of causes and explain fruits, there are both the noble and the ordinary; the two adornments of merit and wisdom must not lack even one.

This is said for the sake of those who are like the blind among the laity, who do not know that there is a path leading beyond the world; it is merely to have them practice meditation and study wisdom, so as to prevent them from losing the two paths of humans and devas.
However, if one is a śramaṇa or a disciple of the Śākya, one must not follow this, for one would be bound by merit and wisdom.
Within the realm of birth and death, one is like a bird with its feet bound by a long rope; there will be no time of liberation. What, then, is the teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
Merit cannot be cultivated, and wisdom cannot be practiced. It is simply that all people must see their nature and realize the Way.
If you wish to see your nature and realize the Way, you must not study any of the Buddha-dharma, nor practice the noble conduct of the Three Vehicles. Merit cannot be...
Wisdom cannot be learned through effort. Thus it is said: "When the Way of non-mind is realized as identical with one's own person, liberation is already at ease.
Sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm shall all together attain perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, one can churn the long river into butter and curd, transform the great earth into gold, and even cause the worlds of the ten directions to become precious jewels—this is not difficult. Why?
"You must certainly exert your spirit to cultivate karmic connections and create merit. Do not take offense at my speaking of such matters.

When I was traveling on pilgrimage in my youth, the venerable masters I encountered all said, 'I do not answer questions; I speak only of dry, withered Chan. They also said, 'Merit and wisdom must not be lacking.
Later, when I saw through this for what it was, I realized I had been deceived by them for a lifetime. Therefore, I—"
While a monk is among the assembly, he does not teach people to study the Buddha or the Dharma, nor does he instruct them to cultivate merit or form karmic connections.
Even so, among hundreds or thousands of people, not one is willing to believe him. This is because they lack the eye of renunciation;

their faculties are shallow and inferior, and they are incapable of faith. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Those of meager fortune and scant virtue are unfit to receive this Dharma. Upon hearing this, [one should understand].
They will certainly lack reverence and faith. If they attain faith, they shall uphold and cause the Three Jewels to flourish; then all sentient beings will have the prospect of liberation.
If they do not attain faith, they will suffer calamity for eternal kalpas. Do not say that this is not the Way. Take care.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Novices and those newly entered into study, have you yet succeeded in leaving the household life? If you have not yet left the household life, you must at least observe the precepts of fasting.
What is meant by observing the precepts of fasting? To harbor a conceptualizing mind is to break the precepts; to seek the flavor [of sensory experience] is to break the fast."
A single moment’s lapse is a great obstacle to leaving the household life. Take care.
[He] ascends the hall and says: "The Buddhas of the three periods appearing in the world praise all people beyond measure.

If I, this mountain monk, were to further provide instruction or guidance, it would be very much like forcing the noble to become base. Nevertheless, even though I have spoken thus, as for the assembly—"
"What is its excellence? Do you know? Examine it for yourself. I shall not detain you long; take care. [The Master] ascended the hall and said:
"Before those who travel the path, what can possibly be said? For why? Nine out of ten words may hit the mark, yet they are not equal to a single moment of silence.
Even though I speak thus, it is much like having already struck with an axe and then reaching out to feel the wound. If one waits any longer for the mountain..."
The monk opened his mouth; this could be called applying moxa to a healed scar. Each of you go down now.
Entering the hall, I shall not ask about the path of Caoxi; tell me, what was it that Maitreya Tathāgata in the Inner Court of Tuṣita was discussing with Mañjuśrī?
Do you see it? Do you hear it? Even if you were to see it directly and hear it directly, it would still be...
Regarding the matter of the Inner Court of Tuṣita: tell me, what is it like on the road to Caoxi? Try to say something.

Do not say that because of long rain the mugwort grows tall; do not say that when spring comes the grass grows of itself. If you rely on such things, it is truly nothing more than a bird’s path or a sheep’s gut;
you have not even dreamed of the road to Caoxi. For those of long-standing study under the former masters, it does not reside in form or words; for later students, it is otherwise.
Beginners must be particularly careful and thorough. I do not ask you to remain standing for long; take care.

When the donor has prepared this vegetarian feast, he ascends the hall. If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of the bright seasonal rites.
Furthermore, as for today’s sublime assembly, all matters are manifest and clearly present before you. But tell me, what kind of matter has been accomplished?
Do you understand? The Dharma is fundamentally not thus; how could it be thus? If one realizes this, it is the radiance of the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
If one does not see clearly at this point, it can be said that worldly afflictions have already arisen. Alas, the Dharma is fundamentally without partiality, yet one perceives distinctions.
It is like the various devas eating from a single precious vessel; according to their respective merits, the color of the food appears different. You, O virtuous one, see...
This is what is called benevolence (*ren*). When the wise see it, they call it wisdom (*zhi*). But for one who has left the household life, what is this?
If you can clarify this principle, then you may take this food; if you are ignorant of this teaching, it will be difficult to digest.
For those who have already attained it, there is no need for further words; for those who have not yet attained it, you must quickly realize it. Be careful.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "People of the great congregation, from time immemorial until this very day, what matter do you have?
Do you know it yet? The Buddhas of the three periods, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, cannot find you.
The beings of the six realms and four modes of birth likewise cannot find you. Even the noble ranks of the three vehicles cannot find you. If one attempts to call out..."
If you treat it as a single thing, it is not fit; if you describe it as being like a single thing, you cannot avoid falling into conceptual restrictions.
Thus, it is said that it "cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*) nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). Even so, this is still merely a name—a mere sketch or carving.
It is worlds apart from the realm of ordinary people. Since it is thus for all of you, what is the use of seeking instruction? What need is there for cultivation?
To act is to rest right where one is; even so, one is still a dull-witted fellow. If you hesitate or deliberate, you are merely deceiving yourself. Take care! Ascending the hall, he said:
"In general, those who study the Way should simply investigate by knocking upon their own selves. Realize that fundamentally there is not a single thing;
realize that before your eyes, too, there is not a single thing. Once you have realized each and every thing, both inside and out will be fully exhausted, and even your own views will vanish."
Such a person is called a "gentleman who has forgotten himself. Thus the ancients said: "In the world today, how many can truly forget the mind?
People like this are the most difficult to find. Though thousands or tens of thousands may study it, not even one or two attain it.
Before you have attained such a state, simply forget the mind and cease all views; remain as if ignorant and as if deluded for ten or twenty years, maintaining this single [state]."
Awakening! Be careful! Entering the hall:
Those who have left the household life discuss reality, not unreality. Therefore the Buddha said: "Having already left the household life, one is like a prisoner released from jail.
With few desires and contentment, do not covet worldly glory. Endure hunger and thirst; let your resolve be fixed on nothing else."
Take care. Ascending the hall:
When the Way prospers, the Son of Heaven’s edict is not transmitted; when the times are peaceful, there is no need to sing songs of great tranquility.
Take care. Ascending the hall: Departing for the Western Heaven, the road stretches ten thousand miles and more. Take care.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, what is there to conceal? Even if one were to speak until the flowers of heaven fall in profusion, how could that compare to the time before the auspicious tortoise has yet manifested its signs?
Even if Śākyamuni had kept his room shut in Magadha, it was for the sake of those with inferior roots and capacities;
even if Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī, it was because he did not consent. And even if he did not consent—this too is but a fox."
Borrowing the tiger’s majesty. [He] descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he says: "O Great Assembly! Today, this mountain monk has presented to you all at once the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
not a single word is lacking. Do not find fault with this mountain monk for his impatience, for it is because..."

I stoop down to accommodate those of inferior capacity. Even if you, O worthy one, were to attain a clear and definitive understanding beneath a single word, and could speak as fluently as clouds or rain—*pfft!* You who eat the spittle of the wild fox! Do not pass before the gate of a true monk.
I strike the master’s waist and break it. Do not say I have not spoken. [The Master] descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he says: "O virtuous ones! In this shared pursuit of study, you must first distinguish between right and wrong.
If you accept things casually, you will spend your entire life in vain. Lately, among those who travel as pilgrims, it has become the custom to go to Tiantai, Huading, or Nan..."
Regarding Yue Shi Bridge: many have mistaken it for the path leading upward. This is merely a place for temporary travel;

it is not the ultimate ground for establishing one's body and life. Furthermore, regarding the "Xuzhou wheat cakes" and the "Zhenzhou large radish," do not mistakenly take these as the sufficient provisions for a free-spirited monk. This is an untimely matter.
This food is for the purpose of luring and guiding the ignorant to stop their crying. From the perspective of a patch-robed monk, it is called "food mixed with poison.
If you have not yet grasped its essential meaning, do not let it touch your lips. If you have already grasped its meaning, you must quickly spit it out entirely.
Should even a hair’s breadth remain in your mind, you will merely be living and dying in vain. Take care!
Ascending the hall, he said: "Unless you rest and simply rest; if you seek the moment of realization, there will be no end to it. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Venerable elders, for what purpose do you travel on pilgrimage? If you wish to have clear knowledge and vision, to thoroughly comprehend both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, and to possess extensive learning, understanding, and skill in question-and-answer, [you must] recognize that [all things] share the same root as heaven and earth and are of one substance with the myriad dharmas."
The Dharma-body and the Dharma-nature—go quickly to various places to study and grasp them.

If you wish to penetrate the Dharma-body and attain the pivotal key of the ultimate, do not let your words be mere descriptions of phenomena, nor let your speech fail to meet the occasion. When anyone comes with a question, do not answer further;
become a free and easy patch-robed monk who does not rely on a single thing. I also request that you go quickly to various places to study this. Even if...

Each and every one of you sees that this has absolutely no connection with the fundamental matter of your own original nature. Therefore, I, the old monk, receive people solely by means of this fundamental matter.

If there were words, phrases, or texts from various quarters for people to apply their minds to and learn, then here in my mountain monastery, I do not establish such words, phrases, or texts, and thus it cannot be learned through the application of the mind; there is no room for you.
This is a place of retreat where scholars from all quarters look toward its shores and withdraw. If you wish to see the fundamental matter, you must not study any of the Buddha-dharma;
you need not investigate any words or phrases. Cease the mind of learning and forget all views and knowledge.
Only when you are like withered wood or a stone will there be a slight portion of resonance. If it is not thus, you are worlds apart from the Way.
"Take care. After sitting for a long while on the dais, he said: "The sword has gone far away; to laboriously mark the boat is in vain. Take care. He ascended the dais and said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot look up to them; the patriarchs of the world have no choice but to remain tongue-tied. To know this—"
Those who already possess this virtue will naturally preserve it; those who do not yet know its existence—what need is there to wait for anything else?
Stop! Stop! Ascending the hall, he said: "Every man possesses a spirit that pierces the heavens. Do not walk where the Tathāgata has walked. Where, then, should you walk?
Come forth, all of you, and speak before the assembly! Do not say it is the South Stone Bridge of Zhaozhou!"
"North! Do not say it is Mount Huading of Tiantai or the Three Peaks of Mount Hua. Do not say it is because people lack far-reaching foresight and must inevitably face immediate anxieties.
If you rely on such a view, it is much like a fierce tiger entering a pit or a swift hawk falling into a cage;
you bring about your own destruction, and the fault is not that of others. Now tell me: what is the path where a patch-robed monk walks? Be careful!"

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Great assembly, yesterday there was a donor’s vegetarian feast. The dignified deportment of the monks and Daoists was majestic; the ritual music of the laypeople was harmonious;
the offerings were abundant; and incense and flowers were arrayed in rows. Such a magnificent occasion as this—tell me, where has it gone today?
If you can know its place of coming, you will know its place of going; only then will you not be bound by cause and effect."
O Kuo, you have attained mastery over all dharmas. If you go toward the mountain of blades, the mountain of blades will collapse of its own accord;
if you go toward the cauldron of fire, the cauldron of fire will extinguish itself. Only then can you roam freely and at ease; what obstacles could there be?

If you have not yet realized this, you will be constrained by the myriad dharmas and have no way to attain liberation. It may be said that your karmic consciousness is busily frantic, meeting with circumstances everywhere and forming [entanglements].
Stagnation. If you encounter adverse conditions appearing before you, how will you dispel them? An ancient said: "Exert yourself; you must bring this present life to completion.
Do not let yourself suffer the remaining calamities for eternal kalpas. Be careful.
He ascended the hall. After a long silence, as the assembly did not disperse, the Master said, "What are you doing? You must not wait for me to douse you with foul water. He then descended.

Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Master Baizhang Heng. At times, when ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly had gathered, he would say, "Have some tea," and then descend from his seat.
At other times, when ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly had gathered, he would say, "Take care," and then descend from his seat.

At yet other times, when ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly had gathered, he would say, "Rest," and then descend from his seat. He frequently used these seasonal circumstances, leaving the multitude unable to fathom their underlying meaning.
[This concludes the] section on the limits. Later, Master Heng composed a verse regarding these three turns of the causal conditions, which says:
"Bai Zhang has three secrets: 'Drink tea; take care; rest. If you can directly accept this, I dare guarantee you have not yet reached the end. The Master said, "Great assembly!"
Take, for instance, when Master Heng composed this verse. Tell me, what was his realization? Do you know where he gained or lost?
If you wish to understand, consider the three occasions he ascended the hall: at those times, he was like a man of integrity.
Yet later, by composing this verse, it was as if he had carved two lines of text upon his face. If one were a person of penetrating insight, they would have understood it the moment it was raised.

Understood. For those of later learning and beginners, it is difficult to discern and distinguish [the meaning]. I, this old monk, shall provide you with annotations from the beginning. Baizhang has three secret instructions:
"The thief’s own body has already been exposed; drink tea, take care, and rest. When the stolen goods are brought forth, one must directly and immediately accept them.
I dare say you have not yet penetrated this; it is much like a judge who holds stolen goods in his possession.

Nevertheless, if you all possess the eye that discerns the Dharma, you will be able to verify it. If, however, you cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, you may be said to be muddled regarding Buddha-nature;
you must consult the wise and virtuous further. It is a pity to live and die in vain. Take care.
Ascending the hall on the occasion of the memorial service for the second anniversary of Master Yin Zhen’s passing, [the Master] said:
"The ancients said, 'Friends fill the world, but how many can truly know one's heart? Let us set aside the matter of knowing the heart; do you truly recognize the person who fills the world?
Master Yin Zhen passed away two years ago, yet I say he is present right now. Do you recognize him? If you do recognize him—"
Master Zhen: Not only throughout the world, but even the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all worthy sages—only here can they be recognized and seen all at once.

Can you see it? Even if you were to recognize and see it all at once, from the perspective of a patch-robed monk, it would still be nothing more than the light of a firefly. Nevertheless, even so, you must actually see it.

Only then can it be attained. Why? If one does not clarify this essential principle, there will inevitably arise the anxieties of gathering and dispersing, parting and separation, as well as the views of birth-and-death and annihilation-permanence. Be careful.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancients said: 'Boundless lands and realms are not separated from one another by so much as a hair’s tip;
ten ages of past and present do not depart from this very moment. Now, when I, this mountain monk, speak thus, does Mount Wulao on Mount Lu hear it?
Why does the Stone Bridge of Zhaozhou not come forth to deliver a message? Even if you were to raise your head..."
"Come! This too is a monkey tying up a pillar. Do not stand for long; take care. He ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time are also thus; all the sages and worthies are also thus; the great assembly is also thus;
and this mountain monk is also thus. But tell me, what is it? There is only the moon reflecting on the wall; there is no more blowing [of the wind]."
Ye Feng. Take care. Ascending the hall:
Under the gate of the Patriarchs, there is simply no room for compromise; before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, what principle could there be?
Even so, those who recognize gratitude are few, while those who betray it are many. *Can* (enter).
Ascending the hall: Under the gate of Dayang, there is no need for a lamp to be lit; before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, how could one even dare to open one's mouth?
Therefore, Śākyamuni shut his room and Bodhidharma sealed his words. But if you come to the gate of Jianfu, I cannot let you pass.
[He] knocks once upon the meditation seat. "Investigate! (Chán).
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "How would I dare to offend those of superior capacity? It is simply because I am bending down to accommodate those of inferior faculties.
Even so, by scheming for another's single grain of rice, one loses half a year’s worth of provisions. *Chan.*

Ascending the hall, he said: "Space has neither interior nor exterior; the dharmas of the mind are likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, this is to penetrate the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the ancestral style of our predecessors; that later descendants have been unable to carry on the lineage is because it is easy to understand but difficult to see.
To understand immediately upon hearing a statement is called 'generating interpretation according to words,' and it is also called 'relying on common knowledge.'"
This "hawk" understands through intellectual interpretation rather than through direct realization and awakening; therefore, his state of doubt does not cease.
This is because he lacks a fundamental basis to rely upon, and his karmic consciousness, busily flitting about, gives rise to heterodox views, saying: "I will not enter this deep pit of liberation."
It is further said: "If you merely run along this Dharma-realm, when will it ever come to an end?
Why not seek an exit? It is also said: "There is naturally a matter of the 'upper grade'. Or it is said: "There is naturally a single path of penetration. What is this path of penetration?
"The key of the character 'Wang' (王) strikes the iron of the guest. Or it is said: "A donkey chooses a damp spot to urinate. Or it is said: "Spring."
The green grass is lush and misty. While they claim to uphold the ancestral gate’s tradition, they instead treat the verbal teachings as the ultimate standard.

This is called "neglecting the mind while valuing the teachings," or "discarding the root to pursue the branches. It is like a dog chasing a clod of earth; for a hundred or ten years, this has been the prevailing custom.
Xuefeng Wushan said, "The Patriarch has been extinguished; you people of today have buried him in the wild weeds.
If one can enter the ancestral gate of the patriarchs, it is like the light of hundreds of thousands of suns and moons, delivering all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
If one enters through words and teachings, it is like the light of a firefly, unable to save even oneself. Why? Because it is dry."

If wisdom does not turn away from [conceptualization], O virtuous ones, you are all equally students. You must cast aside words, letters, and intellectual views, and investigate your own fundamental matter.
Only when you treat the Buddha’s teachings and the Patriarchs’ instructions as if they were born enemies will you begin to have even a slight degree of resonance with them.
Now tell me: what is the matter that constitutes true resonance? Take care.
Upon ascending the hall, as soon as the drum sounded and the assembly had gathered, the Buddhas of the three periods of time were moved to speak with one voice.

I have chanted this for all of you; it may be said that there is no dharma that is not encompassed, no meaning that is not complete, no phenomenon that is not revealed, and no principle that is not made manifest.
Do you all see it? Do you hear it? If you see it, you see the Buddhas of the present. If you do not see it—
If future Buddhas were to exist, then dharmas would possess the extremes of annihilation or permanence, and Buddhas would possess birth and extinction.
How then could the Buddha have said, "All dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unextinguished"? If one can understand it in this way, the Buddhas will always manifest before one.

Nevertheless, although this is so, it must be seen with one's own eyes to be attained. I do not accept mere verbal cleverness from you. If you merely study it, you will not succeed; you must awaken to it.
It is realized within the mind and expressed through speech; thus it is said that one speaks according to realization.

Every word and every phrase is true speech, real speech, suchness-speech, non-deceptive speech, and non-contradictory speech. If one’s vision does not reach this point, then whatever one says is great falsehood—deceiving oneself and deceiving others.
Hereafter, the tongue shall surely be pulled out and plowed with a furrow. This Dharma-gate is... [in]... 109b.4. (The text continues with the title of the scripture.)
Although the realization of those under the Gate of the Patriarchs may seem shallow and mundane, if an ordained person does not perceive it, they are called "blind from birth" or "deaf from birth.
On the occasion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* assembly, such people were judged to be hungry ghosts; though standing by a river, they do not see the water.
Even if they should see it, it all turns into fierce fire or becomes pus and blood. Why? Because this is the matter within the sphere of these individuals' own experience. It is entirely...
In the midst of daily life, if you can see it, it is entirely identical to the untainted wisdom-activity of all Buddhas;

if you do not see it, it is merely the inverted deluded thoughts of an ordinary person. Thus it is said: "The supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is prized by the world, yet when encountered by such people, it turns instead into poison.
Outwardly they are dazzled by sounds and forms, and inwardly they are deluded by what is seen and heard. This may truly be called...
Karmic consciousness is in a state of constant turmoil; how can one repay the four debts of gratitude?

Though you may have studied the matters on the Buddha’s side, this too is a case of the wandering monk misapplying his mind—how much more so regarding worldly dharmas! When the four elements fall into discord all at once, what regret will avail?
That those who have left the home life receive prostrations from their parents and are revered by humans and devas, yet fail to realize the path beyond the world—this may truly be called...
Vainly receiving offerings of faith and unworthily receiving respect, I cannot help but wonder: when Yama, the Lord of Death, cuts the thread of life, what will my own mind be like?
*Chan.* Entering the hall, [the Master said: "Before those who have traveled the pilgrimage routes, it is difficult to open one's mouth to say:

'Do not seek from the Buddha; do not seek from the Dharma; do not seek from the Sangha. For the sake of those practitioners still in white robes, even if they were to destroy the Buddha and slander the Dharma—"
They are merely counted among the multitude; they are still but the disciples who sweep and sprinkle for the Patriarchs.

Even if one were to cut off the world, encompassing the ten directions, with a physical form that is perfectly accommodating, acting as both host and attendant, and pervading all existence in its total containment—though this may be the ultimate proclamation of the Perfect Teaching, under the Patriarchs it is considered the work of those who play with shadows. Therefore, the Old Monk says:
The Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot look up to them; the patriarchs of the world are rendered tongue-tied.
O worthy ones, if you are willing, you still do not possess the eye of the traveling mendicant; if you are not willing, you likewise do not possess the eye of the traveling mendicant.
Tell me, what is this "eye of the traveling mendicant"? Examine!

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Now, those who have left the household life are for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned Dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.
Lately, those who have left the household life have become greedily attached to blessings and wisdom, which is entirely contrary to the Way.

If one seeks blessings and wisdom, one must apply the mind; but if one wishes to realize the Way, there is no need for you to apply the mind. Therefore, I constantly advise everyone: do not study the Buddha-Dharma; simply..."
Cease your mental activity. Those of sharp faculties will attain liberation at the moment of hearing; those of dull faculties may take three or five years, but at the farthest, no more than ten.
If you do not awaken to the Way, this old monk shall send you to the Hell of the Plucked Tongue. *Chan*.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "The summer retreat is drawing to a close. Have you attained resonance with that which occurred prior to the empty kalpa?

If you have not yet attained such resonance, what can be done about this eternal cycle of saṃsāra? What state of mind do you have for studying the Buddha-dharma and extensively seeking intellectual understanding?
Driven by the winds of intellectual understanding, you are blown into the ocean of birth and death. If it were merely intellectual understanding, you all—"
Throughout past lives, you have studied extensively; you possess great knowledge and understanding, and your eloquence and wisdom surpass those of others.
Your mental acuity is swift and sharp, yet it is because your mind has never ceased its activity that this does not accord with the reality prior to the kalpa of emptiness.

Consequently, you have wandered through the cycles of the evil realms for aeons as numerous as motes of dust, no longer possessing a human body. Now, having been born into this world, you have finally attained this human form once again.
Beneath the *kāṣāya*, though you may seek understanding extensively as before, you will be unable to still the mind.
Failing to escape the cycle of the six realms, you will pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. Why not cease the mind and depart? Depart like one who is dazed or lost;
depart for five or seven years without speaking. After that, even the Buddha will be powerless against you. Investigate!
Ascending the hall: Buddha to Buddha, hand is passed; Patriarch to Patriarch, it is transmitted. Guard and uphold it well; do not allow it to be severed.
*Chan*. Ascending the hall: This year’s Dharma-cycle is nearly at its end. We rejoice that the assembly is peaceful and well, and that the gates of our monastery remain tranquil.
I further hope that you will hold the Way in your heart. However, for those who have left the household life, material gain and sustenance must never be their primary concern;
thus it is said: "Having left the home to propagate the Holy Way, one vows to deliver all beings. In ancient times, there were three reasons for leaving the household life:
first, for oneself to transcend the cycle of birth and death; second, to ensure the succession and flourishing of the Triple Gem so that the Buddha-Dharma may long abide in the world; and third...

For the sake of the six realms and the four modes of birth, one causes all to attain liberation. Therefore, one severs affection and parts from kin, renounces honor and nobility, and even abandons kingdom, city, wife, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, leaving the household life to propagate the Way. These three conditions constitute the heavy responsibility of those who have left the household;
they are matters pertaining to the station of the renunciant, which others are unable to fulfill. Observe what has occurred recently...
As for those who have left the household life: which of them worries that their own spiritual power is insufficient and thus forgets artifice and quiets their views?
Which of them desires to perpetuate the Triple Gem and practices according to reality? Which of them vows to deliver sentient beings, not sparing even their own body or life?

If one does not leave the household life for these three reasons, it is of no benefit; one may be said to fail the Fourfold Debt of Gratitude above and to bring shame upon the Three Realms below. Even if...
If you wish to benefit yourself and others, you must first understand how to practice before you can succeed.
If you apply your mind to practice, you may either fall into heterodox schools or enter the stages of the three vehicles; neither of these is ultimate.

Therefore, I constantly exhort all people to first realize their own true nature prior to the empty kalpa, and then proceed to practice from within that realization. If you wish to realize the empty kalpa...
Regarding one's own affairs from the past, one must simply bring the mind to rest. If one attains a state of no-mind, saṃsāra is forever severed.
If one attains no-mind, that is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is itself the Dharma; the union of Dharma and Buddha is called the Saṅgha. This very essence is the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
Even if space were to change, this Dharma would remain constant. Thus we know that only by being without mind can one attain Buddhahood.

This is the life-span of the Dharma. If one attains the state of no-mind, one illuminates and perceives all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, such that they all equally attain perfect enlightenment and all sentient beings are delivered.
Among the gates of practice, resting the mind is foremost. Therefore, the Buddhas of the three periods of time all attained the realization of their nature only upon the path of no-mind.
Regardless of how many three incalculable eons you spend practicing the six perfections and the myriad virtues...
If one practices in this way, one will ultimately not perceive a [fixed] nature. Only when one attains the state of no-mind does one begin to realize the Way.

Therefore, know that no-mind is the path traversed by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Those who have left the household life today should not merely study the Dharma; they should simply learn to let the mind rest.
This is precisely walking the path of all Buddhas. *Can* (conclude).
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma-year since my arrival here has now come to an end.
Venerable Elders, if you travel to various regions and someone asks you about the Abbot of Jianfu, how will you respond? Do not say, 'I was born in the year of the Male Wood Horse;
this year I am seventy-one. Do not say, 'When walking, my feet tread upon the earth; when sitting, my head bears the heavens. Do not say—"
Sometimes they speak of the Buddha and the Dharma; sometimes they disparage the Buddha and slander the Dharma.
At times they untie the bonds and remove the adhesions for others, becoming a free and easy patch-robed monk (*kāṣāya-dhara*) who does not rely on a single thing. Is it not so?
Is it not the case that one cannot say "it is thus," nor can one say "it is not thus"? Is there no place for you to apply your teeth? Is it not the case that one says...?
The question was not yet finished when Lan-zai clapped his hard palms, brushed out his sleeves, and walked away.

"If you communicate and express yourself in such a manner," [the Master] said, "you have not seen me at all. So, how will you communicate and express yourself? If you can see me, speak to the assembly!
After a long silence, he said, "If you cannot speak to the assembly, do not say you have seen me when you suddenly arrive at other places. Take care."
Small Assembly Record:

On one occasion, as the Master was entering the room for private instruction, he said, "Recently, while speaking with you brothers, I observed that when you speak of the principle of 'mind-only,' every single point you make is entirely correct;
you truly grasp the underlying logic to the full extent. It is precisely when you reach this point of questioning—"
To speak of the affairs of other worlds is impossible in general terms; you should know that this must be realized through the mind alone.
Venerable Elders, regarding this matter, one must first attain awakening. If it were someone who has already awakened, even the disclosure of a single message would be different from yours.
What connection is there between such a person’s speech and mere intellectual understanding? Have you not seen the story of Master Shuilao?
A monk asked Mazu Daoshi, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu kicked him in the chest, knocking him to the ground.
When Shuilao rose from the earth, he suddenly attained great realization and said, "The myriad phenomena and the hundred thousand subtle meanings!"
Simply upon the tip of a single hair, you shall recognize the fundamental source and essential nature.
Observe how those who have attained awakening reveal their message; it is truly extraordinary.

Sometimes, venerable seniors, you see brothers coming forward and speaking of principles that seem perfectly complete and rounded, yet when questioned about matters of other lands, they know nothing at all. O worthy ones!
The ancients spoke clearly to you: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. How can you not understand this? They further said:
"All dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind," extending even to the sun, moon, stars, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all do not transcend your own mind.
O worthy ones, why do you not take that very mind which daily pursues the various affairs of the world...
Body and mind: investigate this kind of matter to its very core. O Venerable Elders, regarding this Dharma-gate, I permit you to apply your minds to investigate it.
Why? Because this is not the Way; it is, above all, a most shallow and mundane Dharma-gate.
I see many of you brothers who, upon seeing such a thing, simply stop there. What is the point of that? Nevertheless, even so—
If an ordained person does not clarify this matter, they remain very far indeed from true renunciation.
If one can perceive this matter, body and mind will naturally and gradually come to rest. Why? Because one is no longer deluded by external objects.
For one who has attained such awakening and entry, what need is there to speak of matters in other worlds, let alone the Buddhas of the three periods of time or any of the sages?
Virtuous one, recognize and perceive it all right here. All the dharmas preached by the Buddhas of the three periods of time are perceived right here;
even the dharmas not yet preached are perceived right here. Do you see? Do you see? Therefore, Master Guoqing said:
"To the south are Xuefeng and Gushan; to the north is Wutai and Mañjuśrī."
"Venerable Zhaozhou asked: 'Do you all wish to recognize it? Recognize it right here! Do you see it? Gentlemen, what kind of principle is this?
This matter has been explained with great clarity across thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises;
one must apply the mind to investigate it before it can be attained. Nevertheless, even if you were to awaken to it and recognize it, as for the realm of the patch-robed monk..."
"Superior? Can you still attain it? You can only become a novice or a probationer sweeping and cleaning under the gate of the Patriarchs.
If you hope to be a true monk (nanseng), the difference is as vast as heaven and earth. Therefore, Master Yunmen said: 'Even if you were to take up a single hair-tip...'"
The entire earth is suddenly and simultaneously realized. Yet, within the gate of the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas), there is a vast difference from the world at large.
O worthy ones, tell me: what principle do these patch-robed monks possess? Do you still not understand? Therefore, I often advise my brothers:
as long as your own fundamental matter is not yet clear, do not study the Buddha-dharma. It is better to remain entirely ignorant than to pretend to understand; thus it is exactly so.
There is no place for you to apply your mind; there is no room for you to force it. Moreover, the words spoken here by this old monk are not the same as those from other quarters;
they are also plain and flavorless, with nothing to chew upon.
To this day, it is hard to find a brother among thousands or tens of thousands who is willing to accept them. As for those who have seen and accepted them—
In the end, one must not rely on others to speak for you. As soon as you know that such a thing exists, you should rest directly right there and no longer engage in further discourse with anyone.
Let your mind become like iron or stone; this is the true monk. Not hanging upon the lips or tongue, how could there be any question-and-answer between us?
He knows himself that it is of no benefit, so he proceeds spontaneously in this way and never forces himself. Sometimes, when seeing...
Fellow students of the Way all say that because the matter of birth and death is great, they intend to study this very thing.

But how can it ever be mastered through such study? The more one studies, the further away one goes; there is nothing other than the stilling of the mind. If even a single thought of the mind is stilled, what further "Way" is there to study?
Mindlessness is itself the Way. If you intend to use the mind to study the Way, how could there be any connection? Therefore, the ancients said:

The Way: when the workings of the mind are forgotten, the Buddha-way flourishes; when discrimination arises, the demonic armies flourish. Brothers, if you are willing to go this path, simply learn to let the mind rest;
there is no other place to learn. From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to the present, all have realized liberation from the three realms by ceasing the activity of the mind.
If you, brothers, do not forget for even a single thought-moment, you will wander through the six paths of rebirth for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
In short, you have not yet secured it. Why? From beginningless time until this very day, it is solely because this single thought-moment of yours has not ceased that you do not accord with the Way.
Brothers, now that you have come under the kashaya robe, you must quickly exert yourselves and look for yourselves: what kind of principle is this? These days, those who study...
Those who, as examples, apply their minds to words and phrases day and night are at odds with the Way. You brothers today should simply learn to let the mind rest;
do not grasp at verbal cleverness. You must act like a fool or an idiot, as if you had just emerged from the womb for the first time.
Above all, you must not retain a single character in your mind; only then will it be possible. As for those who study now...

People today are not like those ancients who, as soon as they realized it was thus, would simply go on in that manner, proceeding consistently like cold ashes, extinguished fire, withered wood, or a stone.
You people of today do not take this as your primary concern; how then can you bring yourself into accord with the Great Matter?
Brothers, if you are willing, then practice in this very way. If you are not willing, then [as for] all those of today—
Just as the Way of Chan was flourishing, people were in a hurry to study and copy it down.
Here, I have nothing for you to grasp, nor do I offer a single word or phrase for you to use as an intellectual interpretation.

I merely distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox for you, so that you may avoid falling into false views. At times, I constantly admonish my brothers with bitter words regarding this Great Matter.
I have not yet distinguished it. For now, do not apply your mind erroneously; rather, realize the matter prior to the empty kalpa.
You must simply let the mind rest. Even teaching you all to rest at this moment is a most difficult matter;
this requires a person of the highest root and capacity. If there were even one person today who was willing to rest in this way...
This old monk is capable of serving others. Yet, among thousands or tens of thousands of people, not a single one is willing.
Venerable elders, if there were even one person willing to go in such a manner, you would not need five or seven lifetimes;
you could immediately deliver all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm and manifest five hundred million bodies simultaneously across worlds as numerous as motes of dust.
Manifesting in accordance with those to be transformed, one delivers all sentient beings.
At such a time, there is no need for you to open these two flaps of skin to preach the Dharma for them. Sentient beings who are destined to hear the Dharma will naturally hear it;

their liberation at that moment is not something achieved through the state of a renunciant or through ritual action. Nevertheless, even though this is so, if you apply your mind in this way, you will not achieve realization.
All of these are matters of naturally attaining the ground through the cessation of the mind.
If there were now a single person who could forget the mind and cease all views, they would be able to extend the life-span of the Buddha-dharma, causing it to abide long in the world.

Thus, future generations would have something upon which to rely, and they would also cause those practicing the Way to know that there is a true cause. For instance, when this old monk was previously among the assembly...

For three or four decades, it has been the custom under the assemblies of venerable masters everywhere to exhaustively investigate words and phrases, or to discuss the interplay of "illumination" and "function.
Later, one personally perceives and breaks through such things; for those in the station of a *nanseng* (monk), these are the very matters at hand.

This is called "food mixed with poison. You may be deceived by this perilous path for an entire lifetime. Therefore, while I am among the assembly, I do not teach my brothers to study worldly affairs.
Even if you possess knowledge, insights, or understanding, when you reach this point, you must absolutely vomit it all up before you can succeed.
If there is even a hair’s breadth remaining in the mind, it is nothing but a life lived in vain and a death met in delusion.
You worthy ones, this being the same study, do not harbor further doubts. The words spoken here will certainly not mislead you;
you must become like a person whose breath has just ceased, you must become like a single block of dull, inert stone. You venerable seniors, do you see such a dull stone?
What understanding could there possibly be? If those who have left the household life do not approach the study of the Buddha-dharma in this manner, they are as far apart as heaven and earth.
What benefit is there in leaving the household life in such a way? One cannot even save oneself; how then can one benefit others?
As for the fundamental matter of each person’s own nature, how could I, an old monk, ever manage to explain it to you? To give rise to thoughts and stir the mind—this is [the root of the problem].
It deviates from the essence of the Dharma. Each person possesses their own fundamental reality, fully complete in every respect, lacking not even a single dharma.
Yet they come here to this old monk, standing with palms joined, demanding that the Master preach it for them. How could the ancients have acted toward people in such a manner?
They spent the winter and summer without ascending the hall even once or twice; it was because those brothers truly knew [the truth].

Furthermore, there is no need for others to speak for you; you must personally understand how to practice and maintain it. This is called the "Superior Man of Rested Mind" (xiūxīn shàngshì) and the "Noble Person of Ceased Intent" (xièyì gāorén).

Such a one is fit to be the seed of the Buddha. O worthy ones, this is no small matter. It is impossible for anyone other than those who have known the lineage of the ancestral masters from of old to be able to act in this way.
For those of arrogant character, it is difficult to establish [this state]. No matter how much you may learn... the eight [liberations]... [it remains difficult].
Ten thousand Dharma gates and hundreds of thousands of samādhis will all fail to save you. Therefore it is said: "Dry wisdom does not exempt one from the wheel of suffering.
At this point, I do not accept your mere verbal proficiency. All you venerable seniors, do not listen further to other old monks who urge you to simply "rest and relax.
Rather, throughout the twelve periods of the day, remain entirely without mind; be like a fool, be like an idiot.
O virtuous ones! Leave others to their own affairs and attend to your own great matter. Do not concern yourselves with the long and short, the right and wrong of others.
At all times, you will fail to distinguish east from west and be unable to differentiate between the defiled and the pure; even after the Buddha has passed away, he will be of no help to you.
Although this old monk speaks thus to you all, I am to some extent deceiving myself. What principle is there for those with clear eyes to perceive?
Even so, one cannot avoid wading through mud and water; I shall explain the path for your sake.
Even if you were to attain great awakening upon hearing a single word from this old monk, would that still be your own personal matter?
In total, you have not yet recognized that emotional consciousness and intellectual understanding are merely making a living within the confines of words and phrases;
