they have no connection whatsoever to your own fundamental matter. It is like casting aside hundreds of thousands of suns and moons to cling instead to the light of a firefly.
Do not be surprised that I speak of such matters for the sake of you all. Having heard this old monk’s explanation, what should you do?
Do you believe it? If you can believe it, then practice accordingly.
Therefore, the ancients said: "This one study is most wondrous and most profound; if you simply possess the heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived. If you do not believe...
Go! Your time has passed in vain; you have lived and died in emptiness. This is because the faculties of all of you are shallow and thin, and you are unable to believe.
For now, you practitioners, simply investigate in this manner. Therefore, Master Yunju said:
"If one intends to accomplish such a matter, one must be such a person. Since one is already such a person, why worry about such a matter? Take care.
The Master entered the room. After a long silence, he said, "If everyone were to disperse right now, how much more direct it would be!
Since you do not disperse, you must have me speak here. Now that I have opened my mouth to speak for you, what is there to be gained from it?"

If we consider it from the perspective of each person’s own nature, what more is lacking? Since beginningless time, one has always been shoulder-to-shoulder with all Buddhas; what else, then, remains to be learned?
It is only because you people forcibly give rise to divergent views and create difficulties for yourselves that you are deluded by the two characters "name" and "form.
Whether they be the titles of "saint" or "ordinary," the Buddhas of the three periods, or the eighty thousand Dharma-gates—[all are but names].
There are hundreds of thousands of samādhis, Buddhas, and sentient beings; these are collectively termed "names and forms" (nāma-rūpa).

If one were to set aside the two characters "name and form," what else would there be? Originally, there is nothing that can be obtained. It is only because all people give rise to thoughts and stir their minds.
Delusively there are birth and death; delusively there is bodhi and nirvana, and thus there are mundane and supramundane dharmas.
One gives rise to all manner of false views, casting aside the empty space of the ten directions to instead make a living within a ghost cave.
Originally one is a Buddha, not requiring you to practice cultivation. Since this is so, what more do you intend to learn?
Go! In general, you must abandon the practice of seeking the Buddha by distancing yourselves from sentient beings. Where is the Buddha? It is simply each of you yourselves who are the Buddha.
To awaken to this is to be a Buddha; to be deluded is to be an ordinary person. Therefore it is said: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being.
Nevertheless, though it is thus, you cannot realize its essence through investigation, nor can you attain it through cultivation. This is...
To cultivate that which cannot be grasped, there is nothing superior to the practice of these various sūtras throughout three incalculable kalpas.

Even when one reaches the fulfillment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and preaches the Dharma like clouds and rain, one still cannot see one's nature (*prakṛti*). Only when, suddenly, the mind is absent does one finally see one's nature.
Looking back upon the previous three incalculable kalpas, one realizes that one’s efforts were in vain and that one underwent toil and suffering in vain.
Practice. There is, in total, no substantial reality. You should know that it does not depend upon your cultivation; there is, in total, no application of mind for you to study.

If you were to apply your mind to study, such a thing would be impossible. Even if one possesses great knowledge and understanding, is able to question and answer, speaks with eloquence and attains realization, and possesses swift spiritual acumen and wisdom surpassing others—regarding such matters as these, all people throughout their past lives have [possessed them].
Though you have studied this before, you have merely managed to avoid the cycle of birth and death; why is this?
It is because you have not yet seen your nature or awakened to the Way, and thus the cycle of birth and death remains unbroken.

From birth until old age, you have only recognized the gates and doors, the shadows and reflections, as your body, without knowing the original self that exists from the beginning, nor knowing that which transcends it.
Regarding the matter of the Way: what connection is there between studying and answering questions based on written words and language?

Even if one copies and memorizes three or five volumes, spending the winters and summers under the guidance of various venerable masters and requesting instruction on every point from the beginning, and then speaks of "upward" and "downward," or of "illumination" and "function" in their vertical and horizontal interplay—how can one thereby become a truly free and easy patch-robed monk? Not so.
Relying on a single thing, he claims his own affairs are clear and manifest;

harboring this within his breast as the ultimate standard, he then desires others to call him a Chan Master so as to open the eyes of future generations. How much he has buried and obscured the ancestors!
This is a mistaken interpretation for later generations, attempting to equate such matters with life and death. Is this even possible?
Even if you were to achieve great realization and great enlightenment, and could speak as fluently as clouds or rain, you would merely have gained a reputation for being a smooth talker.
One moves further and further away from the Way, calling it the "lustful woman with signs of greed. Therefore, Master Deshan said:
"Passing it from one mouth to another, it is acquired through lust until it becomes slippery and slick; what benefit is there in this? It is also called a wild fox spirit or a demon.
O virtuous ones, you should know that this matter does not lie within your deliberation or calculation; it is, directly and immediately, this very thing.
Only those who have left the household life can attain this. How could it be taught to you so that you might easily practice it or casually master it with body and mind?

The various sages of the past possessed unimpeded wisdom regarding matters that cannot be reached by conceptual construction; how could such things be contained within your single question and single answer?
Even if you were to cause heavenly flowers to rain down with every single word and phrase, it would still have nothing to do with your own true self.

How much less so when you rely on your fixed views and possess a certain level of intellectual understanding, taking that as your own realization? You would then consider your studies complete, feeling utterly satisfied and fulfilled.
Clinging to a sense of victory and defeat within your body and mind, you go everywhere seeking people to say, "I understand Chan; I understand the Way," merely displaying your cleverness.
"Running wild! To claim, 'I am a guest under the Gate of the Patriarch'—such as these, I call them all nothing but the spittle of wild foxes, the kind of hungry ghosts and heretics.
What kind of practitioners of the Buddha-dharma are they? Lately, among the brothers who study and practice..."
This is precisely what is meant by "each generation being inferior to the one before. They do not know the fundamental matter of leaving the household life at all;

they simply seek to learn how to respond verbally. Fearing that others might question them and leave them with no way to answer, they focus their minds exclusively on words and phrases for ten or twenty years, doing nothing but making a living inside a ghost cave. They do not realize there is a fundamental matter, according to their own learning.

To possess intellectual acuity and understanding is not an obstacle; one may have extensive knowledge and be able to provide explanations for questions. One may thoroughly comprehend and master the phenomena of the world.
Yet, if one fails to gain any real power within the gateway of birth and death, what is the use of such learning for a wandering monk?
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, one will inevitably be blown by the winds of conceptual knowledge back into the cycle of birth and death.
Within the sea, what end can there be? O worthy ones, each of you men possesses a spirit as vast as the heavens;

why then do you bury yourselves here, sinking away? This matter is largely due to your initial resolve not being upright and your being confused by others’ instructions, who told you, "This is right," and "That is not right. Ultimately, you have never encountered a true person. You—
This very nature of one's own self is like space—formless and signless. What kind of face does it have?
How could you possibly attempt to create something to perceive it? How could anyone ever point it out to you?
Even the Buddhas of the three periods of time, though endowed with the five eyes and six supernormal powers, have never seen it; they have never recognized its face since beginningless time.
Up until this very day, there has never been birth and never been cessation; there has never been existence and never been non-existence.
It is only because you have been deluded for a long time that you falsely perceive birth and cessation, and falsely perceive saṃsāra; thus you see phenomena as subject to annihilation or permanence.
Since beginningless kalpas, all of you have never been apart from this single thought-moment—do you still know this? Throughout all this time, this...
Has this single thought ever ceased for even a moment? It has never ceased for even a single instant.
This is why one wanders through the six realms of rebirth for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, no longer attaining a human body; it is solely because this single thought does not cease.
Now that you have emerged from the depths of existence and found yourself beneath the *kāṣāya*, how much more direct and easy is this path! You shall not be obstructed by karmic hindrances.
[One is] constrained by these things. This is precisely the time for right practice. Now, as I instruct all people in practice, how should one practice?
Is it by instructing all people to apply their minds and study the Buddha-dharma? Is it by instructing all people to investigate the causes and conditions of the past and present?
Is this a case of question and answer? Is it perhaps to teach people how to cultivate merit and establish karmic connections?
Here, we do not require you to accomplish tasks, nor do we delight in your verbal dexterity—your ability to ask questions and provide answers. It is none of these things at all.
How much more so for you people, who at the very least lack such things. The general intent is simply to have you all come to rest.
If you do not abandon all previous knowledge, views, and understandings by suddenly letting them go through the cessation of the mind, it will certainly not be the Way;
it will only deceive you all, causing you to waste your body and mind to no avail, and ultimately nothing at all will be accomplished. I urge you all:
It is better to rest and let go. There is no place for you to apply the mind. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, simply act like a fool.
Let things flow naturally and freely, with a mind resembling empty space—even without the measure of "empty space. Only then will there be neither ignorance nor darkness.
As years pass and seasons change, when not even a hair’s breadth of "Buddha-dharma" remains within body or mind, only then is it attained. If there is even one...
If one does not forget even a matter as small as a hair’s breadth, then one’s entire life has been spent in vain. Therefore it is said:
"To learn the matters on the Buddha's side is also a misplaced use of the mind; one must simply be without affairs, and only then can one attain the same state.
Although this is so, it is nonetheless difficult to find such a person—not only now, but since ancient times it has been difficult to find them; how much more so [in the present].
Nowadays, those who study the Way are all led by ignorant, old, shaven-headed slaves into the weeds of delusion. Thus it is said:
"My eyes were originally upright; they became crooked because of my teacher. You younger brothers must all regard the matter of birth and death as paramount.
To benefit and deliver sentient beings, one travels from a thousand villages and ten thousand miles to seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Yet, when such a person is pointed toward by an elder who has no fixed abode, they are taught to apply their minds day and night to study, chasing after words and following along with phrases.
From error to further error, this continues until today, generation after generation, all following this same pattern. Now, you—
That you all have encountered Jianfu’s appearance in the world and that he has spoken such matters for your sake—you should truly rejoice.
At present, there is no one else in the world who can speak of these things; this is no empty boast.
Good people, if you were merely to step outside the gate of Jianfu, there would be no one left to speak of them, let alone anyone who even knows of their existence.
Why? What this old monk has seen throughout his life is something that people in the world today do not know.
If I were to remain silent and not speak further, it would be as if my entire lineage were extinguished. Now that you have all arrived here, you must not pass your time with ease or indifference.
Apply your own eyes; do not allow others to deceive you. Only when you see Buddhas and Patriarchs as if they were born enemies will you have attained it.
At this point, what should be done? Brothers, unless you choose not to study, if you do study, you must investigate with great precision.
You must not accept things casually or understand them too easily, thereby wasting your time without achieving anything real.
You must know that such a thing exists. Aside from this state of no-mind, there is no other path. You must simply proceed like one who is ignorant and deluded before you can succeed.
O worthy ones, follow the way of others by acting as if ignorant and deluded, sinking into emptiness and lingering in stillness; just go about with no affairs.
After five or seven years, or even longer, what is there that cannot be attained? When you finally attain it, at that moment there will be nothing left.
Having attained it, one departs with it; let all dharmas be as they are. There is nothing that does not harmonize.

This is called a "brand new place" where the ten thousand dharmas are fully present. How could you possibly exhaust them through study? Even so, it is impossible to find a single person nowadays who is like this.
O virtuous ones, except for those who, throughout the twelve periods of the day, are like a solid iron ball without a hole.
Only when you have struck it away can you attain it. You must truly allow the Buddhas of the three periods and all the holy sages to fail in finding your tracks;
only then will you succeed. If there is even a single thread of a thought regarding the Buddha-dharma or any divergent notion, ghosts and spirits will immediately see you and recognize you.
In the past, Chan Master Hongjue of Yunju visited Master Wuben of Dongshan. Later, he entered the mountains to dwell in a hermitage;
every fifteenth day of the month, he was required to return to pay his respects to Dongshan. One day, Dongshan asked him, "Hermitage Master,"
"What do you have for bedding, fire, and food in your hermitage? The master of the hermitage replied, "I have none of these.
The Mountain Master asked, "What do you eat every day? The master of the hermitage said, "Every day there are worthies and sages who bring food for me to eat."
The abbot did not understand and was struck by Dongshan’s shout: "I took you for someone of substance;
why have you come to this? The abbot joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "I do not know what fault I have committed.
Dongshan said, "If you have done nothing, why did the sages and worthies send food for you to eat? The abbot replied, "When I was..."
Inside the hermitage, at one time, he was reflecting upon the Master’s words and phrases. The Master said, "You may know this.
Thereupon, the Hermitage Master returned to his dwelling and prepared tea and food for himself. At that moment, the Holy One again brought food, yet the Hermitage Master was nowhere to be seen.
From this point on, I will not send it to you. O Venerable Elders, even the ancients of old, when their body and mind had reached such a state, were still seen by ghosts and spirits;
how much more so for you people of today, who deceive yourselves day and night? The dragons, gods, and local deities see every one of your maneuvers;
whether good or evil, they recognize them all. It is because of this single thought of yours that...
Forget it. This is the general point: you must simply cause this mind of inquiry to cease and this mind of cultivation to cease.
Be like a block of inert stone; be like cold ashes and extinguished fire. If you can do so, you will attain the state of resonance.
If you cannot, then even if you practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds until the end of the future, [it will be of no avail].

If you practice at the very limit, you will only attain the level of a reward or transformation Buddha. As it is said: "The reward and transformation Buddhas are not the true Buddha, nor are they the ones who preach the Dharma.
You should know that this is not easily attained. Now that all of you have arrived here, do not let the moment pass by in vain.
Furthermore, learn to bring rest to body and mind; thereafter, you will naturally become different.

If you can rest this single thought-moment, you will have a slight measure of the qualification for renunciation and a slight measure of the qualification for studying the Way. There is no other place to apply the mind.

Even if you were to master the eighty thousand dharma-gates and a hundred thousand samādhis, and speak them until they filled the dragon palaces and overflowed the ocean treasuries, as far as your own portion is concerned—
In all cases, such a thing is impossible. Therefore, the Buddha said: "It is as impossible as blowing air into a fishnet to make it full; there is no such possibility.
Studying the Buddha-dharma does not consist of this kind of principle at all. Thus, under the gate of the Patriarchs, they simply speak of forgetting words and stilling views.
When Bodhidharma came from the Western Land and arrived here in this soil, he remained for nine years.
Facing the wall, he did not utter a single word. How do you all intend to understand this now? Gentlemen, there is nothing for you to exert yourself with except to bring the mind to rest;
apart from that, there is no other place for you to apply effort. If you can proceed without a mind, you will stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas. A Buddha is simply a person who has no mind.
As for spiritual powers, wondrous functions, all gates of wisdom, and everything else— [Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end.]
As for the gates of practice and all gates of meditative concentration, they are all inherently complete from the very beginning;
not even a single dharma is lacking, nor are they things to be attained through your cultivation. They are all realized by stilling the mind.

Since you have not yet attained this state, first realize the matter of your own self prior to the empty kalpa. Therefore it is said: "People of the present day must have the Great Function manifest before them."

Furthermore, when people ask, "What do you call 'great function'? do they not, upon being thus questioned, immediately come forward to offer greetings and then return to their positions, or perhaps strike a blow or shout a "ho"? To call such things "great function" is precisely the work of a wild fox spirit.
Do you all wish to recognize great function? That which existed prior to the empty kalpa—that is what is called great function. If you realize its essence...
Only when one attains knowledge of events prior to the kalpa of emptiness does the Great Function manifest before them;
only then can they attain mastery within the realm of birth and death and remain unbound by karmic obstructions. Such a person is one who has truly seen their nature;
they possess, at least in part, the Buddha-dharma of body and mind. Observe how those who have attained the Great Function are free in their coming and going. There was the monk Zhizhi who said:
When the Paper-Clothed Ascetic arrived at Caoshan, Caoshan saw him and asked, "Are you not the Paper-Clothed Ascetic? He replied, "I dare not say so.
Caoshan said, "What is the reality beneath the paper clothing? He replied, "A single ball hangs upon the body; the myriad dharmas are all thus.
Caoshan said, "What is the function beneath the paper clothing? The Paper-Clothed Ascetic stepped forward, gave a shout of acknowledgment, and then stood there and shed his skin.
As he was leaving, a monk brought the matter up in the Sangha hall. A second-ranking seat (the *dìèzuò*) heard this and also left.
After a long while, Zhǐyī returned and asked Caoshan, "What is it like when spiritual awareness does not rely on a womb?
Caoshan said, "It cannot be attained through subtlety. Zhǐyī asked, "What is subtlety? Caoshan said, "Not borrowing what has been borrowed. Zhǐyī then paid his respects to Caoshan.
Having finished, he returned to the Sangha hall and passed away while seated. O worthy ones, this man has finally attained the manifestation of the Great Function (*mahā-vyavahāra*).
But as for you all, have you also attained the manifestation of the Great Function? If you have not yet attained the manifestation of the Great Function, you must simply rest;
there is no place for you to apply the mind. There is only the resting of the mind—this is called the foremost.
In studying the Way, if you attain for a single thought-moment a state of no-mind, you cannot be found within the triple world; heaven and hell cannot constrain you.
Like empty space, you have no fixed location. Why is this so? It is simply because you have forgotten that single thought-moment.
Even the Buddhas of the three periods and all the sages and worthies do not know where you have gone.
How much more so for those in the six realms and four modes of birth! It is as if they search for you but cannot find you.
Some attain resonance by momentarily stilling the mind; others only attain resonance after three years, five years, ten years, or twenty years.
Observe how difficult it is for our contemporaries, my brothers, to attain resonance with the Great Matter. Although we say, "The matter of birth and death is great," [it remains elusive].
Thus, one must travel on foot to study and seek instruction. For instance, you brothers, throughout the twelve periods of the day, where do you practice?
Where does that single piece of mind and body reside? If you wish to learn this matter, you must be one who does not abandon the mind and body in order to study;
only then will it be possible. What is meant by "not abandoning the mind and body"? Throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is not a single [moment of]...
When the thought arises, it is called "not abandoning the Way," for such a person’s body and mind are present.
A person like this—one who could be found among tens of thousands or millions—is impossible to find. Therefore it is said: "It is like a person who always lives at home;

they do not worry that the affairs of the household will not be managed. Yet, despite this being so, there is not a single person willing [to acknowledge it]. If, right now, there were truly someone willing to be thus...
"Go! I, the old monk, shall provide him with water for washing his feet. Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "I would not decline the toil of providing the four requisites;
even ten thousand taels of gold could be spent upon him. O virtuous ones, do not speak only of ten thousand taels of gold;
even if you were to take the four worlds and turn them into gold every day, it would still be enough to purchase such a person. He is called the Supreme Being.
According to the Way of the ancients, if even a single person were willing to proceed in this manner, such a person would be the most difficult to find in all of heaven and earth.
This person is pure and without admixture, fit to be a vessel for the Dharma. The brothers who study today, however, ultimately refuse to do so;
they fall into emptiness and instead merely run outside of words and phrases, seeking intellectual understanding and desiring only to gain explanations and ask for clarifications.

Answer: Furthermore, there are old bald monks from various regions who possess no true understanding. They bring disorder to families by corrupting men and women, leading them into brothels where they engage in sexual acts with their mouths.
I point this out for future generations: these people seek to be called "Elders" (*sthavira*) so as to find a way to establish themselves.
Such a band of followers should be called "prostitutes"; what kind of renunciants are they? This is how it should be regarded.
Was the First Patriarch not your equal? Yet, upon arriving in this land, he did not employ even a fraction of that same approach.
Was it that he lacked skillful means, wisdom, or insight? It was simply that there was nothing to be said from his mouth;
it was because he wished to provide no benefit to later generations that for nine years he merely sat facing the wall, never uttering a single word. As for you all—
Above all, do not seek for others to speak on your behalf. What is the use of speaking? You must personally turn the light back upon yourself and reflect:
"What is this principle? Although this old monk has spoken such matters for you all, it must still be that your own minds fully comprehend them before it will suffice.
If you do not fully comprehend them, it will be difficult to settle into them regardless of how you proceed.
Furthermore, this depends on you being able to trust as a human being; this is a teaching difficult to believe. Why is it difficult to believe?
Herein, there should not be a single word or half-sentence to lead people to understanding, nor is there a single message to give to people.
It simply requires that each person examine themselves and investigate. If, in my presence, there were even the slightest bit [of something to grasp]—
The Buddha-Dharma’s knowledge and vision teaches all people how to achieve understanding, like piercing everyone's nostrils and tying them to a pillar.
One must possess the eye [of wisdom] to succeed; if your own eyes are clear, this old monk cannot deceive you. You must fix your own eyes upon it yourself—do not be deceived by others.
To study the Buddha-Dharma to its ultimate conclusion, there is nothing else to do but to rely on oneself.
Only when you have attained true conviction can it be realized. Once you have attained such conviction, all myriad dharmas will fail to disturb you;
your body and mind will naturally become firm and solid. This is what is called the "mind that moves forward. Even the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot call you back from there.
Gentlemen, each matter rests with you individuals. What I, this old monk, say here does not interfere with that either.
"Profitable! These may indeed be called words of sincerity, yet I fear you will not believe them. If you could truly believe them, you would simply let your mind rest for three or five years;
even though others have been wandering through the six realms of rebirth since beginningless time, passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they have still managed to get through it.
Now that I am teaching you to let your mind rest for only five or seven years, in the end you are unwilling to do so."
What is the place of salvation? In the world today, one truly cannot find a single person who is "mindless. Let alone a mindless person, even those who have "rested their minds" are non-existent.

Those who stir their thoughts and give rise to mental activity while studying the Buddha-dharma are as numerous as grains of sand, yet not a single one has awakened to the Way or seen their true nature.
You should know that this is difficult to attain. For the past hundred or two hundred years, we have not heard anyone speak of it.
Attached to this matter, you lead one another further onto the path of error. For a thousand lives and ten thousand births, you will simply pass away in vain.
As for the matter of your own self, it is fundamentally without deficiency;

it is only because you give rise to thoughts and stir the mind that you create your own separation and your own contradictions. This matter is not something achieved through your efforts or practices.
It is attained. Nor is it to be found in the cessation of the mind. It is not like this at all. To speak of "all things being manifest" is merely to add a head upon a head;
how could one speak of generating thoughts, stirring the mind, or seeking through words and phrases? Have you not heard it said: "To conceive a thought is already to err;
to stir a thought is already to deviate"? Now, my brothers, simply practice non-mind. If you attain non-mind, then—
However, know that there is going; you have attained a single thought-moment of resonance.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot find your traces, nor can they establish you anywhere. This time, even the Buddhas do not know you, and the Patriarchs likewise do not know you.
What can possibly be done to you? Therefore it is said: "This person is like a great tiger."
Extremely evil! Furthermore, having grown wings, what place is there to resist? The Buddhas of the three periods of time have no way to emerge before him;

how would they dare open their mouths in his presence? To tread upon the heads of the patriarchs and Buddhas all at once is called the Dharma-body emerging from its bonds. It is like a lion king not bound by a golden chain. Why is this so? Because...

Having attained the way that transcends the world, one is able to personally verify and realize the state of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and receive the seal of approval from the ancestral masters throughout the land.

While it would be a mere trifle for one’s own person alone to achieve liberation, within the entire dharma realm, both sentient and insentient beings alike shall together attain perfect enlightenment.
This time, by virtue of your single person’s power of awakening to the Way, all sentient beings shall have all their karmic obstacles and hindrances completely extinguished.
They shall attain liberation in this very moment and never again enter the three miserable realms from now on. They shall dwell eternally among humans and devas, receiving supreme and wondrous bliss.
He has attained ultimate Buddhahood. Do you think that the functioning of you all can likewise achieve this?
Even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages have limitations when it comes to saving sentient beings;
however, for one who has awakened to the Way, those saved are countless and without end. O virtuous ones, every monastic possesses such inconceivable liberation.
It is simply that the efforts of all people are insufficient to construct it; therefore, they do not know it exists. I constantly exhort my brothers:
"If you have not yet settled your own affairs, what state of mind do you have for studying the Buddha-dharma?
What state of mind do you have for extensively seeking intellectual understanding? You must first realize the reality prior to the empty kalpa. When you have realized this...
Matters prior to the kalpa of emptiness are already settled; you must practice for yourselves and maintain this for yourselves.
There is no need for you to grasp at body and mind—you will naturally proceed in this way. Therefore it is said: "If you attain the root, the branches follow of themselves.
Why exhaust your spirit seeking and trying to understand? This matter belongs to your own domain; go seek it there.
One must not abandon it, nor can one obtain it; it is only when the body and mind are free from grasping and rejecting that one may attain it.

One must truly reach the point where all notions of ordinary and holy are exhausted and even one's own views are forgotten—this is called a person of transcendent capacity who knows the matters of the ancestors.
This must be not engaging in question and answer with you. Only in this way does one possess the true body and mind of the Buddha-dharma.
O worthy ones, all are equally ordained and all are equally engaged in study; do not let your time pass in vain. Time does not wait for man;
each of you must realize it for yourselves. Do not wait until, in a state of agitation, fear, and terror, you find yourselves with no place to go—at that time, it will be too late.
It is difficult to bring order to one's own hands and feet; you must exert effort yourself. How do you exert effort?
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, remain like a single block of solid rock—this is precisely where you all must apply effort. Grasp the matter that existed prior to the empty kalpa.
Here there is no place for your artificiality. Therefore, when this old monk speaks in such a manner, he does so to converse with you all;
it is because your faculty of faith is shallow and inferior that I cannot help but speak here and there.
How could the ancients have been like this, requiring everyone to speak point by point? As soon as you realize it is thus, you can find rest; do not seek further.

This person is capable of turning back [from delusion]. They are like cold ashes, extinguished fire, withered wood, or a stone. Having spread out their bedding in the Sangha hall, they forget to receive their meal;
having received the meal, they forget to eat. Consequently, their hair grows long without the intent to shave it, and their robes become torn without the intent to patch them.
At all times, they are truly unable to distinguish east from west or you from me. This is such a person.
For the first time, you have obtained the very breath of one who has left the household life. Since the ancients of old engaged in study, they did not seek awakening within words and phrases.
Gentlemen, the matter rests with your own self; it does not reside in the minds of others.
Simply set aside all written characters and spoken language, and examine for yourself what principle this is.
If you can examine and penetrate this point, you will not be deceived by the patriarchs and Buddhas. Nevertheless, even so, you must realize it for yourself before it is possible.
You must carefully distinguish right from wrong; first of all, do not accept it casually. If it does not yet accord with your realization, simply rest.
When you rise each morning, food and clothing will be provided freely; there is no need to apply effort. There is one...
I provide for all people; it is precisely thus that I go. Yet, I go entirely without mind. It is unnecessary to cultivate karmic connections or create merit;
these have no real substance. Even if one were to daily provide offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would not constitute an offering.
Even if one were to daily construct as many jeweled stupas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would be unnecessary to build them. What idle matters they are!
Do not let minor causes and conditions obstruct the great matter; simply stop right here. Do not think back or look ahead; just go on like this.

Later, even the Buddha will be unable to do anything for you. Although this old monk ascends the hall every morning and gives a small discourse in the abbot’s quarters every evening, though I speak with bitter words to exhort my brothers, in the end there is not a single word or phrase that can be given to you.
Everyone understands this. No matter how much you run up and down, there will never be a single message to give to anyone.
It is simply because I wish for everyone to come to rest and find peace. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Cease the mind, reach the source, and awaken to the unconditioned Dharma.
O worthy ones, even the Buddha speaks only thus. If you can have faith, then practice accordingly.
"If you do not believe, you will depart [from this life]. It is not only I, the old monk, who cannot save you; even the Buddhas of the three periods of time could not save you. Be careful.
The Master entered the room and said, "Last night, for the sake of my brothers, I brought up the story of Master Yunmen while we were walking along the corridor."
When he arrived below the triple gate, he saw a water buffalo. At that time, there were several monks present.
Yunmen asked, "How many years old is this water buffalo? The assembly of monks could not fathom the meaning.
Yunmen said, "You all should simply ask the old monk; I will speak on your behalf. Then a monk came forward and asked, "How many years old is the water buffalo? Yunmen replied, "Six."
13. Next, it is recorded that Minister Chen Cao was appointed to the governorship of Muzhou.
He went there to visit Master Muzhou. One day, the Minister arrived late; upon his arrival, he said, "Today I was playing ball with the assembly, which is why I am late.
The Master asked, "Is it people playing ball, or horses playing ball? The Minister replied, "Horses playing ball. The Master asked, "Are the people tired as well? The Minister replied, "They are."
Zhaozhou asked, "Is the horse exhausted? Xuefeng replied, "Exhausted. Zhaozhou said, "The pillar [nǚ]. Xuefeng was speechless and immediately descended from his seat.
For an entire night, he could find no peace in sitting or lying down; his mind was anxious and his belly felt feverish. At the third watch, suddenly there was a point of entry.
He waited until dawn and then went up to the Abbot’s quarters. Upon seeing the Master, he said, "Last night, I received the compassionate instruction of a saying from the Master.
At that time, I had no words with which to respond to the Master; now, however, I have one. Zhaozhou said, "The person kicks the ball;
the horse kicks the ball. The book says 'the horse kicks the ball. Zhaozhou asked, 'What about the person?'"

"Is it 'kun' (困, entangled/distressed)? The scripture says 'kun'. Master Zhou said, 'The horse returns because of the 'ou' (否, negation). The scripture says 'kun'. Master Zhou said, 'The pillar [is exposed].
The scripture says 'kun'. Master Zhou then ceased speaking. Venerable ones, tell me: what is the principle here?
Last night I raised these two cases to have you all investigate and examine them. Today, I see that my brothers have arrived."
I am expelling this news. Even according to what you have said, it is not yet the whole picture. Here, too, there is a distinct point of view.
You have not yet grasped the meaning behind Master Yunmen’s question regarding the water buffalo, nor have you grasped the meaning behind Master Muzhou’s striking of the ball.
Why is this so? It is simply because, in the end, you, Venerable Sir, have not seen this field of land.

"You have not yet realized the fundamental source of all phenomena. O worthy ones, if those who have left the household life do not penetrate such matters as these, how can they find peace day or night?
They will be deceived by the lanterns and the pillars; they will be confined within the monastic halls and the Buddha halls.
Nevertheless, even if you were to see each and every thing with absolute clarity and precision, it would still remain within the patchwork robe."
As for the "Superior Division of the Sangha," people still generally call it "running outside in a state of madness" or "matters on the side of reflections.
These have no connection whatsoever with your own self. Now that you have recognized the original source, you are indeed a person of immeasurable capacity;
yet, once you have recognized it, do not take it as a matter of achievement. Set it aside for a moment and you must instead realize the void of the kalpa before time.
Only then can you begin to understand the matter. If you simply stop there, what kind of realization have you achieved?
If you all recognize the water buffalo, you will not only recognize the water buffalo, but even the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
the teacher and disciple, father and mother; and the Buddhas of the three periods and all the holy sages—all will be recognized at once. Only then will you attain oneness with heaven and earth.

The Root: All phenomena are of one essence. If you do not recognize the water-buffalo, then even though you gather with teachers, disciples, parents, and all the holy ones every day, you will fail to recognize them entirely. Why is this? Because your vision does not reach them;
you have not yet realized that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only. Consequently, you fail to recognize all conditioned dharmas whatsoever.
Not knowing the fundamental source of the myriad dharmas, it is said: "Furthermore, one does not know what is fire and what is the house, nor how one loses them;
one merely runs back and forth, looking only for one's father. O virtuous ones, you must simply study and thoroughly comprehend such matters as these.
Therefore, the sages have said: "If you wish to realize the principle of non-arising, you must understand the present."
The preceding matter was merely a coarse and shallow teaching. If your insight does not reach this point, what kind of renunciation is it?
How can you study the Buddha-dharma? Why? Because you do not understand the phenomena before your very eyes; you are deluded by external conditions.

The ancients of old also employed many skillful means to provide guidance for future generations. They told you that the mind is like a master painter, capable of painting all the phenomena of the world.
All phenomena that arise are merely manifestations of the mind; there is not a single phenomenon that does not manifest from your own mind.
All are painted into existence by your mind; there is not a single phenomenon established of itself. O virtuous ones!

When you arrive here, what should you do? In moments of leisure and with no other business, take up the words and phrases of the ancients and investigate them from every angle to see what principle they embody.
This matter is something you can certainly learn through diligent application; if you pursue it day and night, there is nothing you will not understand.
Once you have attained it, do not treat it as merely an achievement—this is simply the first step toward realization.
This is a general matter. Even within the school of the Patriarchs, there remains one further barrier.
In the past, when an attendant of Venerable Zhaozhou announced, "The Great King is coming," Zhaozhou stood up, bowed slightly, and said, "Ten thousand blessings to the Great King.
The attendant replied, "He has not yet arrived at the main gate. Zhaozhou said, "And yet you say he is coming. O worthy ones, what kind of talk is this?
The Principle. Now tell me: did Venerable Zhaozhou at that time recognize King Zhao? Did he see him?
Every day, all you brothers come here in such a great clamor; yet if suddenly asked, "How has his meditation seat been lately?
not a single brother among you can offer a word of response here. You should know this is no easy matter. All of you—!
O Benevolent One, how much more so regarding this matter—what kind of gradual progression could there possibly be? Indeed, among hundreds or even tens of people, not one or two can truly see it.
Even though this is so, suppose you were to perceive each and every aspect with complete and utter clarity.
Within yourselves, sirs, what is there? To call this anything at all is to mistake a reflection for one’s own head;
it has absolutely no connection with your true self. Nevertheless, if you can see through this, I grant that you possess the single eye of a monk. Examine! Be careful.
The verse says:
"Knowledge and views—do not sing of them! Mo, mo, mo! Great man, why such great error? Without cause, you chew on the saliva of wild foxes until your belly is full of knowledge and views."

There is no place for attachment. Even if one manifests in a dream and returns home, one remains transcendent beyond all things, needlessly deliberating. The provisional essentials of the "Double Mystery" allow for both vertical and horizontal mastery;
the sharp edge of the pivot, whether moving with or against the flow, flashes like lightning. It is just like a mad ghost throwing the mind into chaos, or a virtuous person struck by a potent poison.
One must listen with discernment and urgently spit it out; only upon waking from this feverish illness does one finally feel relief. This applies regardless of—

Between Japan and the Western Heavens, what need is there to speak of Mount Sumeru being overturned? In vain do you deceive yourself with narrow views, and falsely gouge out the eyes of the Chan lineage.
Such loyal words are harsh to the ear for the ignorant; let those who are truly accomplished hear them and bear their censure.
No, no, no. To open one’s mouth toward you is already a mistake. Yet you ask again—no, no, no. A lapis lazuli vase filled with filth;
the flavor of nectar turns into poison. No, no, no. A wild fox in a thicket of thorns; having fled into the wilderness, it is caught again.
Upon pure ground, a corpse lies across the road; the head of celestial demons and external paths is tilted and distorted.
Mo mo mo! The nostrils of the Buddhas of the three periods are long; the eyelids of the six generations of patriarchs are thin.

To add a point to an arrow-tip—to make it even sharper than sharp. Leave the chatterers to their empty jesting. Even the hundred thousand and eight thousand *yojanas*—how can they compare to my "mo mo mo"?
The Master has a verse for the official:
A single sheet of white cloud goes and returns; Two sheets of white cloud come and go.
White clouds come and go thousands of times; The vast void abides nowhere. Abiding nowhere, responding to conditions as they arise—does this have a basis? With earnest diligence.
Among those who witness the report, the Buddha and sentient beings share no different path.
As the "Cowherd's Song" arises, daybreak approaches; donning the straw raincoat and bamboo hat, he leans against the gate. Having mounted the ox, he enters the wild weeds.
East, west, south, and north—he wanders everywhere. Old and weary, let him chew on greens and yellows as he pleases. The sun is high and the oxen are full;
it is well to return home blowing the reed flute crosswise. Eating wheat porridge and sour gruel to one’s heart’s content, he rubs his muzzle and mouth and collapses with his robe.
Only a true lion cub among the Dharma heirs can let out a lion’s roar; then all beasts hide their tracks and even the elephant kings flee in haste.
Frost and wind spread across the earth, and the stars and constellations shine brilliantly in the heavens. Why is this so? A third eye has opened, and his mouth has grown wider.
To the Official Who Requests a Verse:
The path is remote and travelers are few; The mountain is high, and the stone image is still. If an official of the court should inquire, Point far toward the midst of the white clouds.
[Presented to Lord Fan Wenzheng]
Each man bears a spirit that pierces the heavens; do not mistake empty fame for defiling your own person. Let go completely and you must stand beyond the thousand sages;
if there is even a hair’s breadth left unexhausted, it remains a speck of dust in the eye.

Departing from this world, heaven and earth share the same root. A bird flies through the sky leaving no trace; snow accompanies the old monk on his journey. Mount Sumeru shakes as the golden staff rings out.
On the fourth day of the winter solstice in the year of Yiyou, a single point of numinous light shines crimson. Take care, you who gather here: Prajñāpāramitā!
The Recorded Sayings of Ancient Chan Masters (Concluded):
Chan Master Chenggu of Jianfu Temple in Ruzhou. His conduct was lofty and pure, and his nature was empty and luminous.
When he visited Chan Master Jingxuan of Daguang, [Jingxuan] said, "He is merely a fellow from within the weeds. He then visited Master Ya of Fuyan, who also said:
He was simply a liberated monk. Consequently, he remained silent all day long, deeply investigating the grand regulations of the former masters.
One day, while reading the words of Yunmen, he suddenly attained awakening. From then on, he lived in seclusion, seeking no fame or reputation.
He took up residence at the stupa of Chan Master Hongjue at Yunju, where scholars from the four quarters flocked to him; thus, he became known as "The Old Stupa Master. Jing...

In the fourth year of the Yuanshou era, Lord Fan Zhongyan was sent out to govern Poyang. Having heard of the Master’s virtue and realization, he invited him to reside at Jianfu Temple to propagate the ancestral style.
A monk asked, "Great teacher of wisdom, with what do you instruct people? The Master said, "Do not. The monk said, "If that is so, then there is questioning and answering.
The Master said, "Do not. The monk asked, "The green bamboo stalks are all True Suchness; the lush..."
"Yellow flowers are nothing other than *prajñā*. What is *prajñā*? The Master said, "In the Yellow Springs (the underworld), there is neither old nor young.

The monk said, "When spring comes, the grass turns green of its own accord. The Master said, "One's reputation shall be imperishable. The monk said, "If that is so, even the blue-eyed barbarian monk would frown.
The Master said, "Step back three paces. The monk said, "It is painful. The Master said, "*Hūṃ hūṃ*. [The monk] asked: "When Linji raised his whisk, the student—"
A monk raised his fist. "Is this the same or different? The Master said, "False words confuse the multitude. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall act according to your command.

The Master said, "To the ends of the earth and the corners of the sea. The monk asked, "One shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function proceed simultaneously. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Dry firewood and damp reeds. The monk then shouted. The Master said, "Blazing flames reaching to the heavens. He ascended the hall for instruction.
Now, those who have left the household life pursue the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned Dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.

Lately, those who have left the household life have become greedily attached to blessings and wisdom, which is entirely contrary to the Way. If one seeks blessings and wisdom, one must first clarify the mind;
yet if one wishes to attain the Way, there is no place for you to apply the mind. Therefore, I constantly advise everyone: do not study the Buddha-dharma; simply [be yourself].
"Rest your mind. Those of sharp faculties will attain liberation at the moment of hearing; those of dull faculties may take three or five years, but not more than ten.
If you do not awaken, I, this old monk, shall send you to the Hell of the Plucked Tongue. (Wudeng Yantong, Volume 16)

Once there was an elderly master staying in a hermitage. He wrote the character for "mind" (心) above his door, he wrote the character for "mind" on his window, and he wrote the character for "mind" on his wall.
Fayan said: "Above the door, one should simply write the character for 'door' (門); on the window, one should simply write the character for 'window' (牕); and on the wall, one should simply write..."
"Wall-character. Xuánjué said: "Do not write the character 'door' above a door; do not write the character 'window' above a window;
do not write the character 'wall' upon a wall. Why? Because the meaning of the characters is already manifest. (From the *Wǔdēng Yántǒng*, Volume 16; the lineage of succession is unknown.)
Preface to the Treatise on the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials by the Ancient Pagoda Master.

The Ancient Pagoda Master composed this treatise to rebuke those of various quarters who merely understand intellectual views but have not yet clarified the Eye of the Way. At first, I was startled by this.
Furthermore, upon examining his treatise on the meaning of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials (*sanxuan-sanyao*), he cites various masters with such clarity that he states:
"How could this dharma-gate be used merely by Linji? It is, in fact, the ritual standard of the Tathāgatas of the three periods.

A monk then asked: "Master, regarding your treatise on the dharma-gate of the Three Mysteries, since there are three names, their expressions must also differ; they certainly cannot be separated from one another."
Linji’s original text states: "Within a single phrase are contained the Three Mysteries; within each Mystery are contained the Three Essentials.
There are Mysteries and there are Essentials—how can these be clearly distinguished? After a long silence, he cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying:
"All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sūtra."
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "Within the tip of a single hair, one manifests jewel-king lands; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
When considering such meanings, it is said that the principle-nature is boundless and phenomenal appearances are boundless; they are intermingled without confusion and blended yet not one.
How could one doubt that a single phrase does not embody the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials? I alone do not understand this [text] by Jin... [the sentence trails off].
Are not the meanings of the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and other such texts forms of knowledge and vision?

Furthermore, since the essential purport of all the sūtras is already complete, how could Linji trace them out and establish his own system? The ancients condemned knowledge and vision, yet their own words contradict this.
How laughable! Chan Master Banzhou Baoji said: "The Way is fundamentally without substance; it is because of the Way that one seeks its name. The Way is fundamentally without name;
it is because of the name that its designation is established. If one says 'this very mind is Buddha,' at present one has not yet entered the profound mystery."
If one says that it is neither mind nor Buddha, this is still merely the ultimate point of following tracks.

Thus, the path beyond—where a thousand sages have not transmitted—is such that students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at shadows. Panshan used these terms to describe the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials;
Yunju said: "It is like a hunting dog following a scent or tracking footprints; what is there to do when the wild goat suddenly hangs from its horns? Do not...
